Our in-depth examination of extremely energetic cosmic rays detected at the Pierre Auger Observatory reveals significant patterns of large-scale anisotropy. By analyzing 93 rays carrying the highest energy, we identified anisotropy signals within predetermined energy intervals. The findings show that these signals exceed statistical probabilities. The direction of these anisotropies is expressed in an equatorial coordinate system called SD, where rights ascension $\alpha$ and declination $\delta$. In the 5-30 EeV range, we discovered two anisotropy signals pointing at approximately (302.3°, -19.3°) and (297.3°, 48.8°) in the SD system. Below 5 EeV, anisotropy signals are less pronounced and show a different orientation at (286.4°, -13.8°) in the SD system. We note that these anisotropy directions may be subject to variations due to the limited number of signals available and therefore might differ slightly between separate groups of cosmic rays. Additionally, we observed anisotropy patterns within individual events composed of multiple air showers. Specifically, we found that the orientation of these anisotropies depends on the direction of the highest energy particle that initiates the shower, a relationship that holds true across different energy ranges and is consistent with an extragalactic origin of these cosmic rays. We also found that the anisotropy pattern is more pronounced in the southern hemisphere, where the anisotropy signal is stronger than in the northern hemisphere. Overall, our findings suggest that extremely energetic cosmic rays exhibit significant large-scale anisotropy and that this phenomenon persists across different energy ranges and geographical locations. We speculate that this anisotropy might be attributed to anisotropic galactic and/or extragalactic source distributions of these cosmic rays, or alternatively, could be the result of mass effects associated with the gravitational potential of the Large Magellanic Cloud. A possible connection to the galactic center also remains to be explored further. Lastly, we observed no significant dependence of the anisotropy signal on the human eye's sensitivity when classifying air showers into different groups based on their energy and orientation. This paper introduces an evolutionary technique-based method for generating quadruped robot gaits that can be applied to a variety of challenging environments. The success of this approach is then combined with reinforcement learning to obtain optimal control policies. By leveraging these two methods, we achieved significant improvements in several key performance markers, including increased rewards, reduced falling rates, and enhanced adaptability to different environments. Notably, our approach resulted in a 75% boost in rewards compared to the existing state-of-the-art method on the Franka-quad dataset, and allowed our quadruped robot to successfully navigate diverse terrain such as steep slopes, rocky surfaces, and sand. By segregating gait and control learning, our proposed framework demonstrates improved data efficiency and enhanced sample quality, which in turn facilitates more effective learning. To validate our approach, we employed the Evolutionary Generator of Trajectories (EGT), an evolution-based generator that utilizes four key metrics to evaluate the fitness of generated gaits. The EGT's robustness, resilience, adaptability, and reward potential enable it to learn from diverse environments, including simulated datasets and real-world recordings, without the need for domain-specific adjustments. Furthermore, our method exhibits superior performance on various evaluation tasks, including compared to other generative models that require extensive hyperparameter tuning. By decoupling gait and control learning, our approach facilitates transfer learning and allows the quadruped to adapt to unseen environments with minimal additional training. With continuous learning enabled, our method achieves a 35% reduction in the falling rate and a 10% increase in rewards after just 200k training steps. Following our approach, we were able to obtain a control policy that earned a 0.83 reward on the flat terrain of the Franka-quad dataset without any prior knowledge, and achieved a 75% increase in rewards compared to the existing state-of-the-art method on the same dataset. Moreover, our method successfully adapted to various challenging environments, including steep slopes (25 degrees), rocky surfaces, sand, and even recovered from an unexpected disturbance while navigating a slope. To validate the efficacy of our approach, we employed multiple evaluation metrics, including the reward, the falling rate, and the samples collected in several challenging environments. By analyzing the sphericity and anisotropy of the emission, we found that both models can be differentiated from each other and potentially identified using future radio observations. Additionally, we created a simulation to demonstrate how to separate disk emission from stellar radiation in observations, and proposed a method for identifying the disk's inner radius. However, a mass loss rate of 10^-9 M_sun/yr would imply that the observed emission can be fully explained by the disk itself. We have also derived a version of the Kalman filter, called the forward-backward Kalman filter (FBKF), for this task. We introduce a new method, dynamically weighted inertial forward-backward (DWIFOB), to tackle structured monotone inclusion problems. By incorporating the forward-backward algorithm and the extrapolation technique from Anderson acceleration, we develop a globally convergent solution that outperforms existing methods. Furthermore, we provide a globally convergent primal-dual version of DWIFOB and show through numerical tests that it surpasses the performance of the Chambolle-Pock algorithm and the Tikhonov regularized Anderson acceleration, while exhibiting enhanced robustness and reliability. Additionally, we offer a locally convergent version of DWIFOB that, under certain conditions, converges at a rate of O((k+1)^-2). We have completed one of the first comprehensive analyses of the complete one-loop corrections to the Higgs boson masses within the non-minimal supersymmetric standard model (NMSSM), incorporating the constraints of minimal inverse seesaw models. Our study specifically examines the role of heavy singlet neutrinos, focusing on two scenarios where either R-parity is conserved or violated. By combining the one-loop corrections with the two-loop corrections, our results offer a more accurate representation of the Higgs sector. The findings demonstrate that the one-loop corrections can modify the tree-level predictions by approximately 3-30%, with the goldstone mode and the lightest neutral higgs mode generally exhibiting the largest corrections. Furthermore, our analysis includes the application of experimental and theoretical constraints, with a particular emphasis on the Higgs signal at 125 GeV, decaying into boson pairs. The study specifically investigates the Higgs mass shifts in relation to the scale of supersymmetry, with a particular focus on the $\kappa$ parameter and the decoupling limit. Based on the Higgs signal at 125 GeV, our results indicate that the $\kappa$ parameter falls within the range of 0.98-$<5$. When considering the scenario of violation of R-parity, our results indicate that the $\kappa$ parameter falls within the range of 0.98-$<3.8$. In contrast, the scenario where R-parity is conserved yields a more restrictive range for the $\kappa$ parameter, with the lower bound increasing to 2. Moreover, our results indicate that the scale of supersymmetry falls within the range of 30-$10^5$ GeV. Finally, our study specifically examines the impact of the one-loop corrections on the Higgs signal at 125 GeV in the scenario of violation of R-parity, with the findings indicating that the loop corrections can modify the Higgs signal by approximately 30% or less. Conversely, the scenario where R-parity is conserved yields a more conservative estimate, with the Higgs signal being modified by approximately 10% or less. The conclusions derived from our study can be applied to a comprehensive range of supersymmetry scales. Consequently, our study offers comprehensive insights into the Higgs sector within the NMSSM, incorporating the constraints of minimal inverse seesaw models and the scenario of violation of R-parity, with the findings providing a more precise representation of the Higgs sector. The emergence of Neural Architecture Search (NAS) has shown great potential in automatically optimizing network architectures. However, current approaches face challenges such as their significant computational costs and the difficulty in generalizing the learned architectures to diverse problems. Our innovative method addresses these challenges by developing a novel synthesis approach that generates architectures based on problem-specific characteristics, utilizing spatial and temporal cues to adapt to various tasks. Our synthesis approach is differentiated from previous methods, such as evolution-based and gradient-based approaches, by its ability to produce architectures that are both efficient and effective. Our results demonstrate improved accuracy and reduced computational costs compared to the hard NAS approach, while our generalization capabilities are superior to soft NAS approaches. Our findings are substantiated by our analysis of the properties of well-performing architectures, which reveals the importance of parameter efficiency, depth, and connection patterns for achieving high accuracy. Our contributions include the development of a Property Guided Synthesis approach and the discovery of meaningful properties for NAS, which can be further explored to develop more effective architectures. Federated Learning adoption has been hindered by communication challenges. A new Federated Learning paradigm, Federated Distillation, has been developed but also faces similar communication issues. Currently, the best communication strategy for Federated Distillation is Local-Model Asynchronous Aggregation, which involves aggregating the distilled models uploaded by clients directly without combining them locally. However, this approach is inefficient due to the requirement for each client to upload a full model. This paper investigates alternative strategies to reduce communication costs. A new aggregation technique called Federated Distillation Aggregation is developed, which involves representing uploaded models through a linear combination of distillable features. This approach requires less communication as it only necessitates uploading fewer features. Additionally, two local aggregation methods, Federated Distillation Aggregation with Label Correction and Federated Distillation Aggregation with Average and Corrected Averages, are proposed to enhance computational efficiency by minimizing the need for each client to upload a full model. These novel aggregation techniques are evaluated on different datasets and found to offer significant communication cost reductions while maintaining comparable accuracy. For example, on the CIFAR-100 dataset, the new aggregation techniques can reduce communication costs by up to 94% with comparable or improved accuracy when compared to Local-Model Asynchronous Aggregation. Similarly, on the ImageNet dataset, the new aggregation techniques can reduce communication costs by up to 97% with comparable or improved accuracy when compared to Local-Model Asynchronous Aggregation. The conventional approach in multi-objective optimization assumes a pre-defined utility function, or it's learned through interactive feedback from the user. An alternative method involves utility function learning, where the user only needs to provide basic preferences. Effective utility function learning can significantly reduce the user's cognitive load, making it a crucial research area. Most existing learning methods require the user to provide complex comparisons, such as 'better', 'equivalent', or 'worse', on a Pareto-frontier representation of solutions. To streamline this process, we introduce a novel approach that allows the user to input simple comparisons involving actual solutions. Furthermore, we enable the user to integrate their personal preferences into the utility function, utilizing the user's preference judgments. By incorporating these preferences, the utility function can be aligned with the user's values. Our approach can be combined with various optimization algorithms and even accommodates additional prior knowledge, such as domain constraints, to inform the search. vulnerable to adversarial attacks, with malicious agents manipulating the
environment to affect learning agents' behavior. To address this issue, we
investigate a new kind of attack where an adversary can't see the learning
agent's policy or its training process. Instead, the adversary can influence
the environment's rewards and observe the agent's reactions. Noting that
existing attacks often rely on having detailed information about the reward
structure, we explore an alternative approach that uses statistical methods
to estimate the agent's long-term goals. Our proposed method uses a neural
network to predict the agent's expected future rewards based on the current
state. By identifying the state features that are most correlated with the
predicted rewards, we can determine the most effective attack strategy. Our
results show that this method can successfully attack a range of reinforcement
learning agents in various environments, such as grid worlds and game
scenarios like Cartpole. What's more, our attacks are highly effective and
transcend simple obstacle-based attacks; they can cause the agents to fall
out of the game in challenging environments like Cartpole. Moreover, our
attacks can be carried out with minimal knowledge of the agent's policy and
can scale to agents with large state spaces. Overall, our study highlights
the limitations of existing attacks that rely on having detailed reward
information and points out the need for more flexible black-box attacks that
can target agents without exposing their policies. Additionally, it shows
that there's no one-size-fits-all approach to such attacks, with different
agents requiring distinct attack strategies. From a defensive standpoint, we
also examine potential countermeasures, such as adding noise to the state
or using robust agents that are less affected by environmental manipulations. From a practical perspective, our study indicates that agents operating in

Our investigation focuses on a 2D electronic lattice from a non-symmorphic wallpaper group.  We find that this lattice contains Dirac points within the first Brillouin zone, which are sensitive to the symmorphic discrete symmetry of the system.  Notably, we demonstrate that these Dirac points can be relocated and the Hamiltonian's topology modified by introducing an 'irrelevant' phonon mode.  This mode, which lacks a direct impact on the system's Hamiltonian, alters the Dirac points' locations when adjusted.  Consequently, this study presents an example where a weak discrete symmetry outcompetes strong interactions in determining the Dirac points' positions, and offers potential avenues for controlling Dirac points through tunnelling.  Additionally, this concept could be applied to create tunable Dirac materials and contribute to the realization of tunable quantum devices via heterostructures.

In reinforcement learning (RL), an agent's interactive decision-making processes play a crucial role. Our research focuses on risk-sensitive reinforcement learning (RRL), which is crucial in numerous real-world applications due to its ability to model an agent's risk-averse or risk-seeking behavior. To investigate RRL's decision-making capabilities, we establish a non-stationary setting, where an agent is reward-sensitive and must adapt to changing environments while completing a series of risk-sensitive tasks. Our key findings include the development of an adaptive risk detection algorithm, which can efficiently identify an environment's risk parameter, and a policy optimization algorithm yielding near-optimal dynamic regret. Notably, the regret analysis showcases the fundamental separation underlying RRL and model-free RL, highlighting the challenges of decision-making in RRL. Moreover, our results are supported by practical design suggestions for risk-awareness and a thorough empirical evaluation. Overall, our study provides a comprehensive understanding of RRL, including the algorithm's ability to adapt to changing environments and complete risk-sensitive tasks with near-optimal dynamic regret in a non-stationary setting. In distributed machine learning, the distributed averaging method is widely employed to facilitate node communication, yet it shows suboptimal performance when dealing with node failures or when the graph topology is irregular. To address these shortcomings, a new class of aggregation functions is introduced that offers greater flexibility and robustness. Specifically, the \emph{Generalized Discrete Exponential Smoothing} (GDExS) family of aggregation functions is developed, which can be tailored to meet specific requirements and is proven to be robust against failures and irregular graph topologies. Furthermore, a demonstration is provided that shows the efficiency of the proposed aggregation function in comparison to the distributed averaging method, particularly in scenarios involving the regression model. The research also introduces a novel procedure for aggregating data using the Krum algorithm, which utilizes the GDExS family and is referred to as the \emph{Filtered GDExS} (FGDExS) algorithm. Experimental results confirm that the FGDExS algorithm achieves superior performance and faster convergence compared to the distributed averaging method. Additionally, the research highlights that the FGDExS algorithm exhibits an exponential convergence rate, which surpasses the distributed averaging method's linear convergence rate. These findings validate the potential of the proposed aggregation function to surpass the distributed averaging method in various machine learning applications. The research also includes code snippets to facilitate the reproduction of the experimental results. The developed code is compatible with PyTorch and SynapseEdge platforms, demonstrating the efficacy of the proposed aggregation function across different environments. The proposed research is believed to contribute significantly to the field of distributed machine learning, particularly through the introduction of the GDExS family of aggregation functions and the establishment of a connection between this family and the concept of categorical algebras. The research also paves the way for the integration of the proposed aggregation functions into widely used frameworks such as SynapseEdge and Parameter Server. The outcome of this research can be applied to a broad range of DSML applications, and the associated code has been already employed in a collaborative research project involving Edge AI in cellular networks. The research has further applications in scenarios involving Edge AI in cellular networks, and the proposed aggregation functions can be directly utilized in such scenarios to yield better outcomes. The connection between the GDExS family and the concept of categorical algebras is novel and offers a theoretical framework that can be applied to various domains beyond machine learning. The research demonstrates the potential of the GDExS family to outperform the distributed averaging method, which has far-reaching implications for the field of distributed machine learning.

A recent framework combining artificial neural networks and mixed integer linear programming for designing chemical compounds has been built upon to create a new method for polymer inference. This new method incorporates a unique way of depicting polymers using monomers, new descriptors that capture their structure, and employs linear regression in the predictive framework. Computational trials have demonstrated that the proposed approach excels in predicting specific chemical properties in polymers, also successfully modeling compounds composed of up to 50 non-hydrogen atoms within a monomeric structure. Furthermore, the approach has been tested on a diverse dataset of 11,840 unique polymers, showcasing its ability to accurately model compounds composed of multiple monomers. To optimize computational efficiency, a proposed 'cut' strategy can be applied without compromising the approach's accuracy. A accompanying online database, PolyDE, has been developed to provide access to the monomers used in this method, along with a detailed implementation guide. This new method has been shown to outperform existing methods in predicting specific chemical properties in polymers. An open-source software package is available for download, allowing researchers to build upon and test the approach's effectiveness. Preliminary research has revealed that the approach can also be adapted for inferring single-chain proteins. This paper presents a unified approach to addressing certain complex optimization challenges in dynamic systems. These systems are characterized by problems that change over time, making it necessary to design controls that are also time-dependent. While there are various methods for handling dynamic optimization, our approach is grounded in a straightforward method known as direct transcription. This method involves converting the continuous problem into a series of discrete optimization issues. What sets our approach apart is the use of high-performance discrete modeling techniques, which enable efficient solutions to complex problems. The paper begins by outlining the general principles of direct transcription before applying this method to a critical problem of ventilator allocation during the COVID-19 pandemic. The pandemic caused a shortage of ventilators, forcing healthcare professionals to make difficult choices about which patients to save. The problem becomes one of optimizing ventilator assignment to maximize survival rates, taking into account the varying probabilities of survival for each patient and allowing the duration of treatment to be adjusted. The results demonstrate that our approach can accurately determine the optimal durations of treatment, leading to improved survival rates and a higher number of survivors. Assuming that the design matrix has a sub-Gaussian structure and that the error variance is unknown, we establish that the posterior mean enjoys a minimax optimal rate of convergence. To achieve this, we leverage a novel result allowing the estimation of the covariance matrix with a rate of convergence of $\sqrt{d/n}$, where $d$ represents the number of predictors and $n$ is the sample size. This finding is of independent interest and holds even in the absence of additional structural priors on the regression coefficients. Furthermore, we investigate the concentration behavior of the posterior distribution and establish a non-asymptotic high-dimensional extension of the concentration inequality for Bayesian estimators. Our analysis also accommodates non-negligent error variance, yielding a characterization of the posterior's concentration behavior around the true coefficient vector. To achieve this, we employ a technique involving "shortening" the posterior distribution by centering and bounding the excess kurtosis. Our approach is versatile and can be applied to a broad range of statistical settings beyond linear regression. Additionally, we demonstrate that the posterior mean enjoys a strong form of concentration, where the rate of concentration is solely determined by the prior's complexity and not the error variance. Our study specifically applies the proposed approach to a real-world scenario involving the hard machining of Inconel 718, which requires precise control of working temperatures and tool tip temperatures. The Bayesian analysis allows for the estimation of unknown material parameters, while the genetic optimization algorithm optimizes the machining center's configuration to meet strict temperature constraints at the tool tip, thereby reducing energy consumption. The outstanding performance of our approach underscores its suitability for optimizing machining operations and minimizing energy consumption in advanced machining centers. This research introduces three indices for characterizing online signature templates based on distinctiveness, complexity, and reliability. 
Distinctiveness is evaluated through statistical analysis and a random signature assumption on a set of user signature examples.
Complexity is determined by examining the features of user signature examples.
Reliability, on the other hand, is assessed by considering a variety of user signature samples.
These indices are used to develop adaptive verification algorithms that can effectively distinguish between genuine and fake signature attempts while minimizing unnecessary verification processes.
Our findings from two signature dataset analyses reveal that our proposed models yield satisfactory accuracy rates and a substantial reduction in unnecessary verifications compared to alternative methods. 
Moreover, our research demonstrates the advantages of our indices over alternative metrics in online signature verification. 
Lastly, our study showcases the benefits of our adaptive algorithms over non-adaptive alternatives and highlights the value of our signature templates' reliability assessment. 
Our research has significant practical implications and could be applied in various authentication systems to achieve faster and more secure transactions.

This review focuses on the principles and advancements of graph representation learning, with a specialized emphasis on its life-saving implications in the biomedical sector. We will examine the challenges of graph representation learning and the substantial impact it has had on the field, highlighting recent examples in areas such as disease prediction, drug development, and personalized medicine. By synthesizing current research and highlighting future prospects, this review aims to inspire innovative applications that can translate graph representation learning into real-world solutions, driving meaningful outcomes in the biomedical domain. Finally, we will make our knowledge accessible through a publicly available resource, including supplementary materials and code, to facilitate reproducibility and enable the graph representation learning community to build upon our findings.

This study reveals that sharing images online can compromise one's privacy, prompting the development of the Content-based Graph Privacy Advisor (CGPA). This system advises users on the level of privacy risk associated with sharing a particular image, based on the similarity between the image and images within an established database of sensitive topics. The CGPA calculates the probability of each image in the database matching the user's image, using a k-nearest neighbor algorithm. For more precise results, the CGPA also considers multiple image attributes and employs a weighted nearest neighbor approach. Following this, the CGPA determines a confidence interval for the matching probability and advises the user accordingly, with a higher risk indicating a stronger association between the image and sensitive topics. Experimental findings confirm that the CGPA's performance surpasses existing privacy systems, while a study in New York revealed that CGPA-flagged images closely resembled actual crime scenes. Notably, the CGPA can operate without requiring the user to specify the domain or identify the image attributes, making it a more versatile system. Furthermore, the CGPA can be fine-tuned for various applications by adjusting its parameters, thus allowing for adaptable and effective image privacy assessments. Ultimately, the CGPA provides a straightforward, user-friendly solution for evaluating the privacy risks associated with sharing images, particularly in graph-based image recognition systems. With continuous advancements in image recognition technology, the CGPA positions itself as a pioneering system in the field of privacy risk assessment. This study investigates the capabilities of color-to-black and white video restoration using an advanced method that leverages learned features from relevant color images. We examined this technique's limitations in the context of videos captured by multiple cameras and discovered that it relies on the assumption that color pixels in nearby frames are closely linked. To overcome the challenges posed by camera disparities, we developed a novel, multi-camera approach based on spatial-temporal keyframe matching. This technique involves matching frames across cameras to identify key images, which are then used to supplement sparse color information for further enhancement of the restoration quality. Given n randomly drawn samples of a complex-valued function, f, from a domain D, under a measure nu, we investigate the theoretical $L_2$ approximation error. We establish that weighted least squares from a finite-dimensional space V, consisting of basis functions phi_1 through phi_n, yields a stable and nearly optimal method with a strong expectation-based guarantee. Specifically, for various distribution assumptions on f, we derive expectation-based bounds on the approximation error, each with a fixed and positive constant, alpha, such that 

E[||f - v_f||^2 / ||f||^2] <= (alpha / (2n)) * [E[|f - <f, phi_j>|^2] / ||f||^2] 

for all j = 1 through n, where v_f is the weighted least squares projection of f onto V. We also examine the average-case behavior and propose a modified estimator that enjoys a strong probability-based error guarantee. Notably, for functions drawn independently from a sub-Gaussian distribution, our analysis reveals that 

P[||f - v_f||^2 / ||f||^2 > C * [||f - <f, phi_j>|^2 / (n * ||f||^2)] > exp(-n / (2 * C)) 

for all j = 1 through n, and some positive constant C. This result implies a quantitative relationship between a function's sample mean and its least squares approximation, where the sample mean can be seen as a biased estimator of the function itself. We discuss the limitations of our approach, particularly its lack of adaptivity, and suggest potential directions for further research. Ultimately, our work provides a fundamental understanding of the least squares approximation, and sheds light on the intrinsic limitations of approximating complex functions with finite-dimensional spaces, a concept with broad applications across machine learning and other fields. 

The research detailed in this abstract draws upon the authors' previous joint work [arXiv 2002.04102]. The main difference between the current and previous research lies in the approach used to obtain the probability-based error guarantee in Theorem 1.1, which has since been revised and strengthened. We have also added several new results and simplified the original proof, while maintaining the theoretical $L_2$ loss framework from our earlier work.

An alternative explanation is that black holes at both ages are more massive on average than previously thought, a hypothesis that's also consistent with the data. To confirm these conclusions, the researchers recommend using future surveys to investigate the mass distribution of black holes in different stages of development. This could help determine whether heavy black holes were present in the early universe and may have played a key role in shaping its evolution. Over the past thirty years, preprints have undergone significant development and growth alongside the expansion of the internet. Since the launch of arXiv in 1991, preprints have increasingly become an essential part of the scientific process, shifting from being a relatively new concept to a fundamental and widely accepted practice within physics and other fields. To understand the evolution and impact of preprints, we have created a database of preprints from the early days of the internet to the present. Our analysis reveals that the preprint movement has experienced steady growth, publishing more articles each year. The number of fields publishing preprints has expanded from physics and mathematics to include biology, computer science, and social sciences. Our database also shows that publishing a preprint significantly increases the citation count of an article, and the benefits of preprints are particularly pronounced in fields that were previously unfamiliar with the practice. To further investigate the growth and adoption of preprints, we have developed a classification system that measures the movement of preprints through three stages: introduction, development, and widespread use. Our results indicate that the timescales for reaching stable use of preprints can vary depending on the field, ranging from under a decade for physics to over three decades for biology. Our data also reveal that fields that were initially slow to adopt preprints are now publishing them at an increasingly rapid pace. Finally, we have found that there is a significant positive correlation between the number of preprints being published and the citation count of research articles. Together, these findings demonstrate that preprints have become an integral part of the scientific process and that they have a significant impact on the impact of research articles. Ultimately, we believe that the value of preprints lies in their ability to facilitate communication and collaboration within the scientific process. As the internet continues to grow and evolve, we can expect preprints to remain an essential component of science. Rather than viewing preprints as a revolutionary change, we believe that the preprint movement is better understood as a natural development driven by technological advancements and a shift in the cultural practices of scientists. Our analysis may hold important implications for fields that are slow to adopt preprints, and we hope that our work will contribute to a greater understanding of the complex and multifaceted nature of preprints. Additionally, we believe that the database of preprints that we have created will be an important resource for scientists and that it may hold significant value for predicting and understanding the movement of ideas within the scientific process. Finally, we hope that our study will serve as a lasting legacy of the preprint movement

Quantum systems have restrictions on their density matrices due to the entropy cone theorem, which states that a subset of state space that includes the ground state must also include a density matrix with the same minimal entropy. We've found that this theorem holds in complex systems when the density matrices are classified by two-dimensional surfaces in higher-dimensional spaces. This formula enables us to compute the crossing mutliplier for models with periodic and semi-periodic boundary conditions. We mathematically establish a relationship for calculating the point spread function of a combined image, obtained by averaging multiple frames with varying exposure times. The formula takes into account the point spread functions of individual images, their exposure times, and weights. Weighted averaging is considered to accommodate non-uniform exposure conditions. The framework is applicable to ground-based observations, where exposure times often differ due to autoguiding techniques using a secondary camera, and to space-based missions, where exposures are typically kept short to avoid saturation and cosmic ray hits. The relationship is then used to define a new measure of uncertainty for a combined image, the standard point spread function uncertainty. The proposed formula is verified through actual data analysis of deep, wide-field galaxy clusters observed by the MegaCam camera at the CFHT, and is found to accurately agree with the results obtained from the application of the Ariew and Lanczos algorithms. The implemented method significantly reduces the computational time, by a factor of 10 to 30, and even more so when dealing with small images. The code is made available for public use. In this research, we address the Cauchy problem for the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations in multi-dimensional space with a wide class of forces that can be written as the sum of a smooth force and a highly oscillating force with rapidly recurring units. Given that the initial conditions and the smooth force have specific properties, we derive key estimates of various measures related to the solution and its derivatives, all based on the maximum norm, providing a fundamental framework for the long-term behavior of the solution. Furthermore, we demonstrate a significant feature - the possibility of the solution's non-uniqueness. Additionally, we formulate two unsolved problems, one of which is a modification of the Fefferman's blade problem. This work is a culmination of the research on the well-posedness of the Cauchy problem in the maximum norm, providing a comprehensive understanding. A special approach was also discovered, which is expected to be useful in future studies. Also, some useful estimates were obtained that can be applied independently. Lastly, some new non-uniqueness cases were found. All these aspects are part of this research paper.

The verification problem for quantum computation is the process of confirming that a quantum device produces the correct output based on a specific input. This step is often resource-intensive and can be a major limitation, particularly when using noisy quantum devices. A recent study transformed the verification process into a classical problem, achieving a significant reduction in required resources. However, the resulting algorithm had a complex time complexity of O(poly(n) log^2 n). This paper presents an improved classical verification protocol with a simplified algorithm and a complexity of O(poly(n)), allowing for more efficient use of quantum devices. This advancement has potential applications in multiple areas, such as extending the reach of quantum-based tasks and finding the optimal point between quantum-assisted and fully quantum-based tasks for maximum performance. Additionally, this research introduces a new concept known as weak classical verification, opening up further investigation possibilities. The updated protocol can be applied to any quantum algorithm, and our research provides a detailed analysis of its effects for several prominent algorithms like estimation and simulation. Our findings reveal that, in some cases, the previously most efficient classical verification protocols still yield better results than the newly improved protocol, especially when noise levels are low. Furthermore, we developed a formula to estimate the noise and release threshold, enabling the calculation of the optimal point for a given situation. Moreover, we explored the potential applications of our research, such as in understanding the behavior of complex quantum systems and identifying patterns in random quantum states. Lastly, we investigated the feasibility of verifying the output of black-box quantum computers and identified several challenges associated with this goal. Overall, our research offers an improved classical verification protocol and contributes to the ongoing discussion of the trade-offs between quantum-assisted and fully quantum-based approaches. Additionally, our research provides a detailed analysis of the complexities and potential applications of classical verification. Moreover, our research introduces the concept of weak classical verification and explores the feasibility of verifying the output of black-box quantum computers. Lastly, our research opens up opportunities for further research into the verification of black-box quantum computers. Generative models of cell shapes have the potential to enable the synthesis of realistic, training data for cell tracking algorithms, as well as to inform biologists about cell development through analysis of modeled cell shapes. However, the complex and varied forms of cells make traditional generative models challenging to apply. To address this issue, we employ implicit neural functions to represent cell shapes, as their ability to define functions in high-dimensional spaces makes them well-suited for this task. Our method, which includes a novel loss function and an active learning framework, has successfully created realistic models of human sperm cells within an intracellular region. Our approach is versatile and can be used to generate cells from three-dimensional image data or from biologist annotations. Our experiments demonstrate that our method produces cell shape variations that are comparable to those generated by a GAN-based approach, while also enabling the synthesis of cells with abnormal shapes when paired with anomaly detection techniques. Our code and sperm cell models are publicly available.

Researchers in neuroscience are striving to uncover the underlying neural code for spatial navigation. Interestingly, a key concept underlying many current neural network models for spatial navigation, including those in reinforcement learning, involves grid cells with unique periodic properties. Surprisingly, recent findings indicate that learning these periodic patterns using reinforcement learning algorithms can be challenging, requiring specific algorithm modifications. These empirical observations lead to two theoretical outcomes: first, developing density-based neural representations may be more feasible than maintaining explicit grid cell structures. Second, incorporating external guidance during training may be necessary to replicate the effective spatial representations observed in animals, such as humans using interactive maps. Consequently, the representations obtained through reinforcement learning are not necessarily direct models of biological spatial navigation. Therefore, researchers should exercise caution when interpreting the outcomes of reinforcement learning experiments as proxies for natural spatial learning processes. Instead, these results offer valuable insights that can be applied to develop more effective neural network architectures for spatial navigation, such as incorporating orthogonal features or stabilization techniques like regularization. Moreover, these findings provide an opportunity to deepen our understanding of the complex interplay between biological and artificial learning processes. Finally, these outcomes may also influence the design of virtual environments for human navigation, such as video games, where the addition of external guidance through rewards or interactive elements can potentially improve learning outcomes and induce more robust spatial representations. Overall, this research highlights the necessity of rigorous testing before drawing conclusions about the representational power of biological spatial navigation systems based on reinforcement learning experiments. By embracing these challenges, we can unlock the full potential of reinforcement learning as a powerful tool for developing advanced spatial intelligence in both machines and humans. Additionally, by bridging the gaps between artificial and biological learning, we can gain profound insights into the underlying mechanisms of spatial navigation representation. Furthermore, this research may also contribute to the development of more accurate brain computer interfaces by simulating the dynamic interplay between different neural components involved in spatial learning through reinforcement learning. To evaluate the efficiency of event-driven molecular dynamics simulations for complex systems such as two-dimensional dipole simulations, it is essential to analyze the characteristics of individual events. These simulations use a model where particles interact only when they collide, and to improve convergence, additional, non-physical interactions are sometimes introduced that dissipate energy over time, making the dynamics irreversible. In the case of complex systems like these two-dimensional dipoles, it is necessary to understand how these non-physical interactions slow them down. Our research involves studying the event creation process used in the molecular dynamics algorithm for a system of hard-disk dipoles and examining the differences between an event-driven method that preserves energy and one that dissipates energy. Our results include the distribution of event creation times, the average number of events per unit time, and the event types for both the conservative and dissipative models. Interestingly, the conservative model reaches a steady-state faster than the dissipative model, and the positions of the steady-state peaks for event creation times differ between the two models. Additionally, the conservative model reaches the steady-state sooner than expected, and the types of events that occur initially are different from the types that occur at the steady-state. Our findings will guide the development of event-driven methods for other complex systems. We present a novel universal method for identifying traveling chimeras and synchronized clusters in neuronal networks with uniform and heterogeneous excitatory and inhibitory synaptic interactions. This approach is robust, easy to implement, and applicable to networks of any size and complexity. It involves measuring the dynamics of a chimera using a fixed density of observed neurons and calculating the order parameter for the community to which they belong. If the network is in a chimera state, this will result in a positive value for the order parameter, accompanied by a bimodal distribution of neuron densities. Furthermore, we derive a relationship for the width of this distribution, which is a function of the network parameters and the number of neurons. This relationship enables the calculation of the phase coherence for chimeras and facilitates a comparison of our method's results with those obtained from other more computationally intensive techniques. Specifically, we find that our approach is capable of determining the stability of chimeras at a fraction of the cost incurred by other methods. Additionally, we show that for a given number of neurons, our method can determine the phase coherence for chimeras at a lower cost than two other established techniques. Moreover, we demonstrate that the order parameter is directly proportional to the size of the cluster it represents and that the distribution of neuron densities is a reliable indicator of chimeric states. Finally, we establish a relationship between the distribution of neuron densities and the distribution of active neurons that underlies a rich spectrum of spatiotemporal patterns, including chimeras, synchronized clusters, and anti-phase states. It is found that chimeras and synchronized clusters are characterized by distinct relationships between these two distributions. Moreover, it is observed that as the inhibitory synaptic interaction is decreased, a transition from a chimera to a synchronized cluster occurs. Conversely, as the excitatory synaptic interaction is increased, a transition from a chimera to an anti-phase state occurs. A novel module is presented, allowing researchers to model complex systems influenced by random forces impacting particle motion, a phenomenon anticipated to occur within environments like turbulent planetary disks and the remnants of planetesimal disks. This module streamlines the creation of synchronized noise with variable intensity and auto-correlation time for each particle, with low memory requirements, and is available at no cost through the REBOUNDx supplementary module suite. Our approach involves generating noise in 64-bit floating-point chunks, which are then divided into smaller sections based on the desired noise duration, thereby eliminating the need for additional memory. Each particle's noise is generated using a unique formula, which helps to create the impression of noise that is synchronized across particles, a feature particularly useful for studying small particle groups. Our implementation is particularly efficient, with the ability to handle millions of particles and thousands of time-steps per second, making it highly adaptable. Our noise approach can be tailored to fit various noise patterns by adjusting the intensity and correlation properties of the noise, which we successfully verified through a series of tests. Lastly, we have integrated our module into the REBOUND module and made it available through the REBOUNDx module suite, which also includes other innovative time-stepping algorithms. Key aspects of quantum science include precise measurement and feedback mechanisms, offering wide-ranging benefits from advanced technology to fundamental research. To leverage these advantages, it is essential to develop precise mathematical models, specifically the quantum linear Fokker-Planck equation, which describes complex quantum systems influenced by measurements and feedback. This equation can be applied to various applications, such as optimizing experimental procedures or uncovering underlying physical processes. To solve this complex problem, an innovative approach is presented, involving the development of a novel stochastic differential equation and the associated quantum conditional probability distribution. The associated stochastic differential equation was formulated using continuous feedback, and the resulting quantum conditional probability distribution was derived from the related forward equation. The proposed method was validated through numerical simulations based on a basic model of quantum measurement and feedback. The results demonstrate that the proposed approach enables the simulation of quantum systems subject to measurement and feedback, thereby facilitating the analysis of their dynamics. Moreover, this approach allows the calculation of relevant statistical properties, such as the quantum conditional probability distribution and the associated moments. The proposed method was verified through numerical examples and is now available for general use in the form of a Python package. However, using behavior IDs is impractical when predicting CTR for new ads without prior interactions. To overcome this limitation, our approach utilizes visual characteristics of ads to enhance traditional CTR prediction models. We introduce the concept of "visual behavior IDs" derived from ad images, which are employed in place of traditional behavior IDs. Additionally, we propose the use of a pre-trained image encoder to capture valuable semantic information from ad images. Our model's extraction of visual features enables the identification of ads with appealing visuals, thereby enabling more accurate CTR predictions. Our approach is particularly effective for predicting CTR of new ads, showcasing improved generalization capabilities. Notably, our model's performance surpasses that of a baseline model by approximately 8.5% and 3.6% in our default and strict evaluation settings, respectively. Furthermore, our model demonstrates improved stability and stronger correlations with actual CTR predictions when compared to the baseline model. The proposed approach provides a viable solution for predicting CTR of new ads, offering valuable insights for advertisers in selecting ads with high CTR potential. The proposed visual behavior IDs also offer a novel means of understanding ad images based on user perceptions. Moreover, our model's predicted CTR rankings were found to be more in line with actual user clicks when compared to the baseline model. The proposed approach has numerous potential applications in advertising and can be readily integrated into existing CTR prediction models to yield better results. while less attention has been given to analyzing the behavior of process participants.
Recent advancements in business process management now enable the definition of case models,
which can represent individuals interacting with processes.
These case models are represented using attribute-based case data models,
which rely on business information models for proper interpretation.
This can be achieved by applying constraints to the available data attributes.
By employing cardinality constraints, it is possible to clarify the meaning of case models.
This technical report outlines a proposed approach for defining and applying cardinality constraints
as well as establishes a method for validating their effectiveness.
A demonstration is provided, using the example of university applications,
along with the necessary background information on business information modeling and case data models. 
Furthermore, the report includes a full-fledged case model for university applications,
complete with relevant discussion. Finally, the report presents a refinement method for case models,
utilizing cardinality constraints as a means of further analysis and improvement. 
This enables more accurate understanding and analysis of the represented individuals. 
The report concludes by outlining potential future research avenues.

Protecting users of location-based services with significant privacy requirements is extremely difficult when multiple locations are shared within a short time frame due to the significant relationships anticipated between these locations. Our proposed R\'enyi divergence based framework measures and bounds expected privacy losses for interrelated data sets, further demonstrated through an algorithm incorporating conditional Gaussian process priors. This framework illustrates the challenges in safeguarding dependent data and provides a strategic approach to maintaining sensitive location data privacy within a specified boundary. Our analysis ultimately confirms the difficulties and limitations in safeguarding highly correlated location data while maintaining user privacy standards. To resolve this issue, users may need to choose between a higher level of privacy or a lower correlation threshold in certain situations. A sample implementation of our framework is also demonstrated in an outdoor navigation system scenario, where maintaining user privacy while navigating may not be possible in some cases due to highly correlated location predictions. Our framework offers a versatile solution, applicable to various location-based service privacy requirements. This research investigates how replications across multiple sites affect the accuracy of predictive models built from resting-state fMRI data and enhances our understanding of statistical power in multisite studies. We analyzed data from 1,814 subjects from 11 sites that participated in the ENIGMA fMRI study, and through cross-validated random forest analysis, derived weights for a universal prediction model. This model was then applied to see if site replication improved outcomes. Results showed that while a comprehensive model had strong predictive capabilities, site replication did not significantly impact its accuracy. However, when we restricted our analysis to each site individually, we found that the cross-validated models performed better on the data from the same site, but also occasionally performed slightly better on data from other sites. We concluded that replication across multiple sites is not necessary to develop an effective predictive model for a common population, but does offer benefits for optimized model performance within individual datasets. Building on previous work, where a directed graph equivalent of the Ricci curvature was developed based on the Chung Laplacian, this note focuses on deriving a characterization of our lower Ricci curvature bound by applying a heat semigroup gradient estimate and a heat flow-based transportation inequality. This will serve as the basis for establishing a concentration of measure inequality for directed graphs with positive Ricci curvature. Notably, our findings will be illustrated through the analysis of two distinct graph models: a directed cycle and a certain generalized version of the cycle, which is akin to the Bergman metric on the upper half-plane, thus revealing an interesting link between graph theory and Riemann surface topology. Furthermore, our method will also be used to investigate the convergence of the heat semigroup in directed graphs with positive Ricci curvature. Lastly, a new inequality relating the Ricci curvature to the eigenvalues of the Schrödinger operator will be presented. We expect this to be a useful tool for exploring the interplay between curvature and spectral properties in directed graphs. On a broader note, our results will also be applied to the analysis of a stochastic process known as the Schrödinger diffusion, which is particularly well-studied in the context of directed trees. We anticipate that our findings will not only provide valuable insights into the properties of the Schrödinger diffusion but also facilitate a more in-depth understanding of the dynamic behavior of the related stochastic process, which is the target of our current research. We look forward to sharing these results in the near future. We will also establish a new inequality that relates the Ricci curvature to the entropy-regularized Wasserstein distance, which will serve as an alternative expression for our existing entropy-regularized Witten Laplacian. We expect this to be a useful tool for exploring the properties of the regularized distance. We will also apply our methods to the analysis of a stochastic process known as the Witten Laplacian, which is particularly well-studied in the context of directed graphs. Using density functional calculations with the PBEsol approximation, we investigate the electronic structure and superconducting properties of the H$_{3}$S hydride under different pressures. From first-principles molecular dynamics, we analyze the isotope effect and critical temperature of H$_{3}$S as a function of pressure. We find that the critical temperature's pressure dependence follows an unusual pattern, initially increasing at lower pressures before eventually decreasing at higher pressures, a trend that can be explained by the movement of a van Hove singularity in the density of states as pressure increases. This increase actually places the singularity at a point of positive curvature in the dispersion, where it has a more significant impact on superconductivity. Additionally, we find that the H-S isotopic mass ratio decreases with pressure and becomes negative at high pressures, a change that coincides with a critical pressure for superconducting H$_{3}$S compounds. Our results indicate that the behavior of H$_{3}$S hydride superconductors near the critical pressure requires careful consideration of the impact of the van Hove singularity. We also note that compounds with lower critical pressures exhibit more pronounced isotope effects and are better candidates for neurotoxin-free hydrogen-based high-temperature superconductors. Finally, we provide a simplified model to explain the pressure-dependent behavior of the isotope effect and critical temperature of H$_{3}$S hydride superconductors. This model highlights the significance of the density of states at the Fermi level and the average phonon energy and suggests that the H-S isotopic mass ratio can be represented as a product of two pressure-dependent components, the electron-phonon coupling and the heat capacity. We hope that this model will facilitate further research into the superconducting properties of hydrogen-based systems. We also propose that experimental investigations should be conducted to verify our predictions, particularly the negative H-S isotopic mass ratio and the critical pressure-dependent behavior of H$_{3}$S hydride superconductors. Moreover, we suggest that the van Hove singularity's impact on superconductivity should be taken into account when designing and optimizing hydrogen-based high-temperature superconductors. This approach could potentially lead to the development of more efficient and environmentally friendly superconducting materials. Finally, we acknowledge that our calculations were performed using a 32 TPA node with computational support from the Texas Advanced Computing Center and the National Energy Research Scientific Computing Center. We also acknowledge that this research was funded by the Department of Energy

However, the mathematical structure underlying this theorem is misleading, leading some to mistakenly interpret it as a mechanistic description of the selection process rather than a statistical analysis of the relationship between generations. We clarify the statistical nature of Fisher's theorem and highlight the differences between average effects and causal influences, demonstrating that the former are not sufficient to determine the latter. Our understanding of Fisher's theorem is rooted in the framework of category theory, which provides a precise definition of the spaces and map functions involved in the theorem. Although our approach adheres to the original mathematical framework, it also seeks to illuminate the underlying mathematical structure. We also examine the average effect, a concept introduced by Lande, which, along with the genetic variance, can be used to simulate the evolution of inclusive fitness. We clarify that the average effect, as defined by Lande, is a linear operator representing the average change in a trait given a specific mutation. Our redefinition of the average effect is distinct from its original interpretation as a measure of the efficacy of genes. We also explore the connection between the average effect and the fundamental theorem of calculus, highlighting the distinct mathematical structures underlying these concepts. This paper outlines our approach to integrating a thruster system with a bipedal robot's existing propulsion technology, with the goal of improving efficiency and reliability in locomotion. By utilizing the thrusters to supplement the bipedal robot's leg movement, we believe we can optimize its walking pattern and achieve greater stability. Our primary objective is to reduce the number of footsteps required between power sources, in this case, batteries, in order to extend the bipedal robot's range between charges. Our approach to modifying the robot's gait and incorporating thruster-assisted propulsion is a key part of this strategy. Our methodology for assessing the bipedal robot's efficiency involves calculating a complex metric that takes into account the effects of various leg movements and thruster powers on the robot's velocity. By using this method, we evaluated several different walking patterns and identified one with significantly increased range between charges. Our system's performance was then fine-tuned using a control algorithm to maximize velocity while minimizing power consumption. Our results show that with the aid of thrusters, the bipedal robot can achieve a substantial increase in range between battery charges. This research presents a visual relocalization technique within a 3D environment, utilizing surfel maps created from video sequences captured by autonomous vehicles or mobile cameras. To generate distinctive descriptors for each image, we employ a pattern-based image representation and a multi-layered convolutional neural network designed to produce descriptors resistant to geometric variations. A probabilistic voting method is developed to estimate a global map's geometry from partial observations, and further expanded to accommodate situations to where sufficient data is not available for a full map creation. Moreover, we propose a framework for combining map information with descriptor similarities to perform either global or local relocalization. Comprehensive experimental results validate our approach's efficiency and demonstrate successful relocalization within both constructed and non-mapped environments. Additionally, our method exhibits a significant reduction in both computational time and memory usage, making it suitable for real-time applications on mobile devices. Details of our method are disclosed with the aim of facilitating reproduction of our results for the benefits of the scientific community. A demo video is available at https://youtu.be/6h4yB0yQx6g and our code at https://github.com/zhengzhiquan/3D-Surfel-Localization can be accessed for review. Decentralized machine learning techniques like federated learning are well-suited for
handling large datasets on various devices and networks. Nevertheless, they often
neglect to account for the diverse data distributions on different devices, which
can lead to underperforming models in certain scenarios. Our study combines this
consideration with the goals of semi-supervised learning - to maximize performance
with a limited number of labeled data, and to minimize the need for such data.
Our novel approach uses noise to stimulate communication among users and
encourages the main model to focus on shared information, while separate 'personal'
models on each device learn the unique characteristics of each user's data.
Our evaluation shows that our technique allows for efficient communication, retains
accurate models, and eliminates the need for labeled data with notable performance
improvements. Our source code is available at https://github.com/MTResearch/PUFSSL.

This research explores the optical interaction between a dimer of dielectric nanoparticles near the graphene layer. By applying a precise electromagnetic model, the analysis reveals that the shared current within the dimer generates a significant electric field that interacts with the graphene. As a result, the characteristic Rabi splitting observed in optically driven nanoparticle dimer resonances is replaced by a notable shift in the terahertz radiation-driven resonances. Our computational findings demonstrate that the graphene's influence can be either amplifying or diminishing, depending on the relative strength of the electric and magnetic interactions. Notably, our model allows for the adjustment of the radiation frequency, particle size, and graphene coverage to achieve optimal coupling. Graphene can be placed either above or below the dielectric dimer to achieve this effect. To better understand emergency department operation, we analyzed the average response curves for treatment times in two hospitals. Our findings revealed that these curves exhibited a distinctive shape, which deviated from the typical M-shaped pattern previously reported. Instead, the data exhibited an S-shaped pattern. Our research used a Bayesian analysis to estimate average response curves for treatment times based on a dataset containing only order information. The results showed that the estimated curves converged rapidly and that treatment times followed a log-normal distribution. By applying the estimated models to new data, we were able to effectively forecast treatment times. Our approach provides a versatile framework for analyzing and forecasting emergency department performance. Moreover, considering the treatment as a categorical variable allowed us to account for the inherent structure and to obtain more accurate predictions compared to traditional methods. Our comparisons with previous studies and other techniques demonstrated that our approach was superior. A open-source implementation of the proposed method is available. Our research aimed to contribute to the existing literature on emergency department operation and provide a useful tool for clinicians and policymakers. Additionally, we explored the applicability of our approach to other real-world scenarios where response curves were unknown or not straightforward. In cooperative systems with multiple agents, coordination enables tasks to be performed that would be beyond the capabilities of any single agent. We will investigate the concept of coordination through a strategic decision-making process that involves mutually supportive actions among agents. To this end, we will analyze a scenario in which agents choose between two actions: a cooperative action that yields no direct reward but facilitates communication with other agents, and a self-interested action that yields a temporary reward. Utilizing a framework of Bayesian games, we develop an approach to determining equilibrium strategies that maximizes the overall system reward. This method involves utilizing regular graphs to model the effects of communication and reward among the agents. We will demonstrate that solutions to these strategic problems can be found through the use of regular graph algebras and network flow problems, providing efficient algorithms and examples of applications. Furthermore, our analysis will reveal the dependence of the system reward on the graph topology, thereby enabling the design of optimal coordination strategies based on graph properties. Additionally, we will explore the scenario in which agents make random decisions, and we will establish conditions under which the system converges to a stable state characterized by regular behavior. This research contributes to the fields of strategic decision-making, control theory, and graph theory, while also offering practical examples and guidelines for design in various applications. Furthermore, our study may lead to the development of new algorithms for distributed systems and new challenges in machine learning and artificial intelligence. Finally, our investigation provides novel insights into the coordination of cooperative systems.

The surge in online fundraising (or crowdfundraising) has created a platform where individuals can collect financial support directly from the public. This unique setup poses research questions about how to successfully secure funding by tapping into the collective wisdom of the crowd. Our cross-domain investigation combines data from two different platforms: Wikipedia, which relies on crowd-sourced funding through the Wikimedia Foundation, and Kickstarter, a leading all-or-nothing crowdfunding site. Our goal is to identify the characteristics of fundraising campaigns that effectively engage the crowd and predict success. By analyzing features such as fundraising goals, content, and donor interactions, as well as the impact of social influences like comments and ratings, our study provides insights into the crowd signals that influence fundraising outcomes in both domains. Our analysis sheds light on the optimal fundraising strategies for both donors and fund-raisers, and reveals key differences between the two platforms that affect fundraising dynamics. Ultimately, our research can help guide fundraising campaigns to better understand and tap into the crowd's decision-making process. Machine learning (ML) based detection of network attacks has become a widely accepted approach. Training a model using a local dataset, however, can result in a model that is not effective due to limited information. Cyber Threat Intelligence (CTI) sharing has become a key solution, allowing multiple parties to cooperate in training ML models. Traditional methods of CTI sharing, based on sharing models or data, pose security and privacy risks. A new approach to address these concerns is the Federated Learning (FL) framework, which enables secure and private collaboration among network operators. This framework allows for collaborative machine learning without exposing sensitive network information. In this paper, a new FL-based scheme is proposed for CTI sharing, allowing multiple clients to cooperate in training an intrusion detection model without compromising their security and privacy. The scheme's performance was tested using the NSL-KIT dataset, and results show that FL can overcome data scarcity issues, improving classification accuracy significantly. Furthermore, experiments using real-world networks and FL demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed scheme in detecting attacks. Our study also shows that the FL-based scheme outperforms traditional ML methods, and that the proposed model accuracy approaches 100% in certain scenarios. A comparison of our scheme with existing FL-based schemes, including DeepHillNet, also shows superior performance. Our proposed FL-based scheme thus offers a reliable solution for secure and collaborative ML-based network intrusion detection. In complex networks, a phenomenon occurs where different clusters of oscillators, comprised of distinct systems, synchronize with their own distinct rhythms. When each cluster contains identical systems, synchronized within that group, but operating independently from other groups, this phenomenon is known as group synchronization. Typically, it's assumed that all systems within a given group have the same properties and are fully connected, but these conditions aren't necessarily necessary. In this research, we examine cases where there are varying parameters among the oscillators within a group and also investigate the effect of inter-group connections that could potentially bridge these divisions. Through both theoretical analysis and computer simulations, we explore the boundaries and versatility of group synchronization. Specifically, we've discovered that even under harsh conditions, such as significant differences in parameters and internal connections within a group, it's still possible for the oscillators to synchronize into separate, distinct groups. In situations where the inter-group connections are weak and don't allow for synchronization across groups, but do allow for communication within a group, we've observed a phenomenon where a leader system within a group can influence and synchronize other systems. Ultimately, our research provides a more realistic and versatile understanding of group synchronization. Moreover, it also opens up opportunities for various technological and biomedical applications where there are multiple groups or clusters of oscillators that need to be synchronized, such as in coordinated robotic arms where a lead device helps to synchronize other devices. Similarly, in the human brain, where different brain regions are connected through distinct pathways, understanding group synchronization can shed light on the synchronization of brain rhythms in various cognitive processes and may also help in diagnosing and treating brain disorders. Finally, it's also relevant to the control of scroll waves in chemical reactors where different patterns or behaviors are connected and may need to be synchronized across different groups or clusters. In conclusion, our research addresses a gap in current knowledge and provides a more comprehensive understanding of group synchronization, thereby enabling a broader range of applications across diverse fields. These operators exhibit intriguing monotremy properties and have important implications in both physical and mathematical terms. By examining the spectral operators, we identify known features of the model, including its scaling spectrum and a specific field with a known beta function. Additionally, we provide new, tighter constraints on the spectrum. Furthermore, we investigate two monotremy defects, focusing on a known duality between the Wess-Zumino model and a free fermion and a new relation involving a Liouville model with a rotonic term. Our analysis yields an exact matching of the bootstrap bounds for the two theories, thus confirming the model's monodromy defect property. Lastly, we provide a mathematical explanation for the theory's analyticity in the central charge space. This analysis could potentially be extended to other 2D CFTs with monodromy defects. The capacity of wireless networks can be diminished by interference, and managing it efficiently is crucial for achieving optimal performance.  Traditional methods either minimize individual link interference or allow it to reach a threshold, but they fail to account for the correlated nature of interference.  In this study, a random medium access control (MAC) scheme is employed to optimize system performance while considering the interference correlation.  A mathematical model is developed to find the optimal probabilities for data transmission and channel switching, and a computational method is derived for finding these probabilities.  The random MAC scheme is shown to be distributed algorithms and can be implemented using the IEEE 802.11 standard.  The results indicate that this scheme can achieve a significant increase in wireless capacity, and outperform traditional methods in specific scenarios.  Additionally, the random MAC scheme can be further optimized by taking advantage of the convex nature of the interference correlation, leading to improved performance.  The findings of this study provide a framework for designing MAC protocols that adapt to varying levels of interference correlation, and can be applied to develop more efficient protocols.  The research also identifies several avenues for future investigation, and the study of wireless interference correlation as a whole.  Furthermore, the study demonstrates that in the specific scenario of K-user interference, the optimal protocol can be analytically determined. Despite the exceptional performance of Graph Neural Networks in semi-supervised node classification, they face significant challenges when dealing with an extremely limited number of labels. The semi-supervised pseudo-labeling method is often employed to mitigate this issue, which aims to supplement the training set with high-confidence, pseudo-labeled nodes in a self-training cycle. Nevertheless, current pseudo-labeling techniques have several shortcomings. Primarily, they rely on a simplistic strategy for assigning pseudo-labels to unlabelled nodes without considering their local neighbourhood structure. As a result, many pseudo-labels lack informative value, leading to unnecessary noise in the pseudo-training set. Furthermore, they often utilize a universal strategy for selecting nodes to be pseudo-labeled, which may not effectively optimize the utilization of the available labels. To address these limitations, we introduce a novel informative pseudo-labeling approach. This involves using a Graph Convolutional Network to produce informative pseudo-labels based on each unlabelled node's local graph structure and assigning these labels only to unlabelled nodes with high local label propagation confidence. Our approach has been extensively evaluated on six datasets, revealing that it outperforms existing pseudo-labeling techniques by a significant margin, with an average improvement of 6.8% accuracy across these datasets.
