As DNA storage emerges as a promising technology for long-term, extremely dense data preservation, existing DNA storage systems often prioritize read efficiency over data update costs, resulting in inefficient use of DNA sequences due to frequent data changes. To address this gap, our research proposes the DNA-R (re)use framework to efficiently manage sequential data updates in DNA storage. The framework enables frequent updates by treating the DNA sequence as a self-organizing tree, allowing us to efficiently insert, delete, merge, and split DNA sequences. Our results demonstrate that insertions, deletions, mergers, and splittings can be performed in DNA-R (re)use in 0.78x to 1.08x the time of B-tree operations, and that updating a sequence with 10% errors incurs only a minor performance decrease while offering a substantial storage density improvement (3.88x to 7.52x better than uncorrected sequences) with minimal correction overhead. Additionally, DNA-R (re)use exhibits a read latency comparable to systems optimized for reads, and allows for a high degree of data coexistence between the original and updated versions, enabling flexible selection of the version for reads. Our experiments also show that using a page-based update approach reduces the impact of frequent data updates on read efficiency while resulting in only a minor increase in update efficiency. Furthermore, by integrating the version chain and path index schemes, DNA-R (re)use can efficiently manage diverse data update patterns and hierarchy structures, and enable seamless data version management. Due to the diverse applications of machine learning, its ability to identify patterns in datasets is well-established, but its capacity to operate efficiently on large-scale, complex datasets is limited by the computational power of its platform. The approach treats origin-destination demand as a stochastic process and estimates its parameters using Bayesian statistics, resulting in a framework that can be applied to any traffic model without requiring additional assumptions beyond the conjugate prior distribution. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through simulations involving real-world data from the Minneapolis-St. Paul metropolitan area, and the findings highlight the importance of considering the stochastic properties of traffic data to avoid underestimating the variability of the origin-destination demand matrix. The simulation results also show that the method can produce reliable estimates of the mean and variance origin-destination demand matrix even when the prior distribution is unknown. The development of this new estimation approach is crucial for enhancing the accuracy of long-term strategic transportation planning and operations planning. The method's applications extend beyond these models, and its estimation framework can be applied to a broad range of domains beyond traffic, such as social networks and biological systems. The well-documented Aldous-Broder and Wilson algorithms create random spanning trees through random walks, and this research examines their synergy with the aim of reducing tree construction time. By synchronizing these algorithms, a faster, two-stage method is proposed that generates random spanning trees in less time. The first stage uses the Aldous-Broder and Wilson algorithms in parallel to prevent early degeneracy and ensure a fair distribution of tree constructions. In the second stage, the two algorithms are run again, this time allowing the trees to develop fully. By switching between these stages, the proposed method not only shortens overall construction time but also makes the process more efficient by generating trees either quickly or with additional features. The research also shows that, in the long run, the proposed method produces trees just as randomly as the individual Aldous-Broder and Wilson algorithms. The new approach has been successfully implemented and the results confirm its performance. The research involves analyzing the results of running the proposed method against the individual Aldous-Broder and Wilson algorithm, demonstrating that it reduces the time needed to generate a random spanning tree by up to 25%. Within a cellular environment, proteins and nucleic acids autonomously separate, resulting in the spontaneous formation of membraneless droplets. This process underlies the development of numerous sub-cellular compartments. In a model system designed to understand condensate assembly, researchers found that mixing proteins in a specific order significantly influences the droplet formation's kinetics. By including a shared protein in the mixing sequence, the model emulates the co-assembly of biomolecular condensates. Analysis of this protocol's effects on droplet formation reveals two distinct phases. In the initial phase, the droplet's volume and number follow typical LSW distribution. In the latter phase, the droplet's volume deviates from this distribution, and the number continues to increase. To explain these observations, the authors propose two modes of droplet interaction: sticking and splitting. A non-conservative force is also considered. The study's results provide insights into the distinct behaviors of droplets formed from shared components and offer a framework for exploring the complex interactions within biomolecular condensates. Furthermore, the research lays a groundwork for investigating the cellular compartments' assembly and the underlying mechanisms of specific sub-cellular compartment separation. The study also suggests possible experiments to verify the proposed theoretical framework. Based on the model's predictions, it is proposed that the droplets formed from shared components can either merge or dissolve, depending on the relative rates of protein exchange. At low exchange rates, the droplets behave independently, following the classical Smoluchowski coalescence model. In contrast, the droplets deviate from this model at higher exchange rates, displaying increased numbers and varying volumes due to the exchange of shared components. In this context, the droplet's persistence is determined by a balance between formation and dissolution rates, rather than its initial size. Therefore, the droplets do not follow the classical distribution, instead demonstrating an increased number due to the exchange of shared components. We've developed a new category of map functions known as oriented colored broken submersions, which are a critical component in Mather's useful form of the Lagrange multiplier theorem. This theorem, in its most basic form, is equivalent to the combination of two key outcomes: the first, known as the Lagrange multiplier theorem, explains how a certain mathematical object, known as a 1-form, influences a function on a manifold; the second, known as the Lagrange embedding theorem, describes the relationship between a function and its tangent map. Together, these theorems hold significant importance across multiple fields, including mathematics, physics, engineering, and engineering design. Our work builds upon the foundation established by Mather, who introduced the concept of oriented submersions in the 1970s, by generalizing the scope to include colored broken submersions. This generalization is a key aspect of the b-principle, a theoretical framework that seeks to apply geometric and homotopy-theoretic concepts to the analysis of practical problems. More concretely, the b-principle asks whether certain abstract mathematical conditions are sufficient to describe the topological properties of real manifolds. Our research demonstrates that oriented colored broken submersions are a suitable candidate for this theoretical framework, thereby expanding the list of eligible map functions. This achievement represents a significant advancement in the field, thereby validating the concept of the b-principle. Moreover, the b-principle has far-reaching applications, including the explanation of topological properties of real manifolds, the generalization of combinatorial principles, and the application of homotopy type theories to the analysis of practical problems. Specifically, the concept of oriented colored broken submersions enables the simultaneous analysis of multiple problem constraints by translating them into a geometric representation, thereby facilitating the generalization of the Lagrange embedding and multiplicative Lagrange embedding theorems, which describe the relationship between a function and its tangent and multiplicative properties. Furthermore, these generalizations hold important implications across multiple fields, including mathematics, physics, and engineering, as demonstrated by the inclusion of several examples in the paper. This research involves comparing the efficiency of Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) and Algebraic Multigrid (AMG) methods for solving complex cardiac mechanics problems on various types of finite element grids. By modeling the mechanical properties of heart muscle using three-dimensional finite elasticity equations, researchers have transformed the problem into a nonlinear algebraic system. A range of detailed models are employed to capture the mechanics, which results in large, sparse systems. Due to the vast number of degrees of freedom involved, solving these systems directly is impractical without the aid of preconditioning and iterative solvers. A novel, scalable BDDC solver has been developed specifically for cardiac mechanics and shows better performance than AMG-based solvers in a range of tests. The study examines how different grid topologies and cardiac model details affect the performance of these solvers, and it also introduces a graphical tool for visualizing the efficiency of BDDC and AMG solvers based on the structure of finite element grids. The research highlights the potential of BDDC solvers to efficiently handle large-scale problems in cardiac mechanics and suggests that they could be an effective tool for future simulations involving detailed mechanical models of heart mechanics. In this study, we conduct a thorough examination of five leading global optimization algorithms as a hyperparameter configuration problem to understand the overall impact of their settings on performance. By utilizing three methods of sensitivity analysis and evaluating various adjustable parameters, such as covariance matrix adaptation, differential evolution, and non-dominated sorting, we analyze their behavior when influenced by different sampling methods and metrics, providing insights into which settings significantly affect performance and interact with each other. The overall findings suggest that these algorithms benefit from adjustments in their internal parameters and that their response to hyperparameters varies based on the chosen optimization criteria, leading to the conclusion that tailored settings are often necessary to achieve the best results. Additionally, we observe that the most effective hyperparameter configurations frequently exhibit a notable 'optimal-control' feature, where they exhibit excellent performance within a narrow range before rapidly deteriorating as the configurations move past their optimal point. Notably, this characteristic is more pronounced in ranking-based evolutionary algorithms and is less noticeable in those that do not use this approach. Furthermore, we find that these ranking-based algorithms tend to have a broader and more variable range of influence when compared to other optimization methods. The overall analysis sheds light on the overall impact of hyperparameters and highlights their intricate interdependence, while also providing general guidelines for their optimal adjustment. Moreover, we provide recommendations for strategies that could improve these evolutionary algorithms and suggest future research directions based on our findings. The focus was on classifying patients who required intensive care, using discrete features derived from the dataset. The aim was to establish a straightforward method to help clinicians assess patient severity, given the limited availability of medical resources and equipment for performing detailed patient evaluations. The study compared two models, one based on decision trees and the other on random forests, both utilizing a standard classifier and another with customized features, along with their respective variants using human-annotated labels from medical professionals. Additionally, combining the need for oxygen supplementation and lung condition severity yielded a higher accuracy than using either factor alone. To expand a dialogue system's capabilities and facilitate its practical use, discovering new intent categories from user inputs is essential but remains understudied. Current methods are often inefficient, inaccurate, and require extensive labeling. We address two key research questions for this challenge by presenting new approaches to represent user inputs semantically and cluster them effectively. Firstly, we develop a multi-task pre-training strategy that leverages a large amount of text data to generate intent labels and semantic representations simultaneously. Pre-trained language models possess the ability to capture grammatical characteristics, making them suitable for tasks such as parsing. Current parsing models are typically custom-designed for specific applications, but our work explores the potential of utilizing pre-trained language models directly. Through our research, we have discovered two approaches that enable unsupervised and few-shot parsing using these models. The first approach relies on the intrinsic self-supervised objectives inherent to language model pre-training, while the second involves introducing an external unsupervised parsing objective in addition to the model's standard pre-training objectives. By combining the benefits of pre-trained language models and self-supervised learning, we have developed novel unsupervised and few-shot parsing models that demonstrate superior performance on traditional parsing tasks, including constituency and dependency parsing, as evidenced by our evaluation results. Notably, our models exhibit particularly strong results on resource-constrained datasets. The source code for our models is publicly available.

In this research, we explore the potential of HS images to streamline image segmentation, a complex task that typically requires substantial annotated data. By projecting these images into lower-dimensional color spaces based on dominant spectral features and then applying an existing segmentation model, we successfully reduce the required annotated data needed for HSI image segmentation while maintaining seamless integration with standard image segmentation methods. Notably, our approach excels in urban settings, as demonstrated by our experiments using the Cityscapes dataset. Our findings are concise and accessible without requiring additional resources. The projected HS images effectively facilitate image segmentation, and our proposed method enables the efficient application of HS images in this context. Moreover, our approach can be adapted for other segmentation tasks and datasets, including those with limited annotation labels. Social media platforms are facing significant problems due to the presence of toxic content like hate speech, off-color language, and misogyny. These difficulties have caught the attention of the Natural Language Processing (NLP) community, driving innovative research in the field. In this study, we report on the performance of our models in the inaugural Arabic Misogyny Identification challenge, where we evaluate three different approaches: a binary classification model, a system that can distinguish between three categories, and a advanced model capable of differentiating between nine distinct types of misogynous content. Our binary classification model relied on Convolutional Neural Networks and achieved a remarkable 99.3% overall accuracy, a task that also leveraged the power of human insight through feature engineering. Our system that can identify three categories of misogynous content employed a combination of CNN-based approach and a Support Vector Machine, while our advanced model capable of identifying nine distinct types of misogynous content was a deep learning model that integrated multiple tasks in a unified framework. Through our combined efforts, we successfully classified 94.4% of the data with high precision, making us the top-ranking team in the competition. Our advanced model will significantly benefit from integration with other NLP systems, opening up new avenues for research in the detection and analysis of misogynous content. Our work has far-reaching implications for the detection and understanding of toxic content, paving the way for further exploration in the detection and analysis of hate speech, off-color language, and other forms of toxic content in the future. Moreover, this research will contribute to the development of more effective hate speech detection systems, given the established link between misogynous content and other forms of hate speech. Ultimately, this will lead to improved knowledge of toxic content, enabling more accurate detection and analysis. We establish a formalization of the Scott model in univalent type theory, and it turns out that it can be done without relying on choice. The key to this realization is that we can define the order on the non-zero elements of a field as a total order that is consistent with its multiplicative and additive structures. The concept of the Scott model has been previously applied to programming languages in a way that is independent of choice, and this formalization has important implications for proof that programming languages remain compatible with intuitionistic logic, even when they include features for handling ungroundable and infinite data. The formalization can be found in the Coq-unicase library. Furthermore, we use this to show that fully certified compiler for Pure Type Systems in univalent type theory is possible, and this provides a new way to understand the relationship between type theory and programming languages. The existence of such a compiler has previously been referred to as "univalent programming", and this research provides a stronger foundation for this concept by separating the issues related to types and their meaning from those related to programming and its semantics. The fact that we are working within univalent type theory also means that we do not separate the types from their corresponding propositions, and instead work with a single level of types that are known to be equivalent to the corresponding propositions. As a result of this, the concepts of types and propositions become interchangeable, and the relationship between them is no longer an issue that needs to be addressed. The formalization can be found in the uniprg library. Direct photons have been measured at $p_T<5$ GeV/$c$ for midrapidity and most central events of Cu$+$Cu collisions at $\sqrt{s_{_{NN}}}=200$ GeV. By calculating the $e^{+}e^{-}$ excess in the $e^{+}e^{-}$ mass distribution over hadronic contributions, we found that the contribution of very low-momentum direct photons increases with the number of participants. Using a function that incorporates both initial-state and final-state effects, we determined the photon yield at $p_T<1$ GeV/$c$. The results indicate that the photon yield at $p_T<1$ GeV/$c$ for Cu$+$Cu collisions exceeds that of Au$+$Au collisions by about a 20% factor for the same number of participants. The results are in line with the predictions of the NLOM model, which attributes 30% of the photon yield to final-state effects. The findings also show that the photon yield at $p_T<1$ GeV/$c$ for Cu$+$Cu collisions is higher than that of $p$+$p$ collisions by about an 8-fold factor. The data have been compared to the predictions of the NLOM and GLM models for various system sizes and energy scales. The results are consistent with the notion that the NLOM model provides a more accurate representation of the photon yield at $p_T<5$ GeV/$c$ for nucleus$+$nucleus collisions. The data have been posted on the website of the STAR Collaboration.

Pulsar halos are large-scale, TeV gamma-ray-emitting structures associated with pulsar wind nebulae. They are thought to be the result of accelerated particles escaping from the wind zone and are characterized by a larger gamma-ray emission radius compared to the SNR. This review focuses on the properties of 16 pulsar halos in the Galaxy, highlighting their spatial and spectral features, and includes a discussion on the potential candidates for new halo candidates. The analysis also explores the possible connection between the pulsar halo and the unidentified TeV gamma-ray sources in the Galaxy. The review further investigates the Pulsar Halo Phase Diagram and the Pulsar Luminosity Distribution, and concludes with an examination of the pulsar halo properties as a function of pulsar and SNR parameters. The data are then systematically compared to the numerical simulations of pulsar halo formation. The overall picture suggests that the observed properties of pulsar halos are in line with the expectations from the theoretical model, and that future simulations need to incorporate a larger number of pulsars to confirm these findings. Additionally, the review discusses the distinct features of pulsar halos, wind nebulae, and SNRs based on their gamma-ray emission, and explores the possibility of a new phase, the "Pulsar-White-Dwarf" phase, characterized by soft gamma-ray emission. This paper addresses the complex task of weather recognition in images. The commonly used WeatherAPI dataset is insufficient for deep learning methods due to its limited class variety. To address this issue, the researchers have developed an extensive multi-class weather dataset comprising 31 distinct weather categories. To enhance the reliability of convolutional neural networks in this context, they suggest employing data augmentation through transformation of existing images. The evaluation process involves rigorous comparison of multiple network architectures using the new dataset, with the aim of determining the most effective design. The proposed approach has the potential to benefit tasks such as autonomous driving and aerial monitoring by utilizing images from low-cost, accessible cameras. A significant drawback of the network architectures evaluated is their substantial computational complexity, which may hinder real-time applications. To mitigate this, the researchers suggest combining their method with the use of a simplified, single-layer network as a potential area of future investigation. A publicly accessible platform has been provided for downloading the new dataset and the source code of the experiments. The results demonstrate that the use of data augmentation and the selection of an architecture with multiple hidden layers are crucial for the optimal classification of weather conditions. Notably, the application of deep convolutional networks has the potential to surpass the performance of more established methods, such as support vector machines, in this domain. A comparable performance was achieved using a combination of primary and secondary features to train a multiclassifier, although this required more computational resources than the deep convolutional network approach. The evaluation process also revealed that the use of a weighted loss function could enhance the robustness of the model when faced with class imbalances in the dataset. A potential area of future investigation is the incorporation of recurrent neural networks to capture temporal dependencies in image sequences. Additionally, the integration of a geolocation module could further improve the accuracy of weather classification in aerial images. By incorporating the latitude, longitude, altitude, and elevation of the image's location as input, the researchers found that a simple multilayer network could be developed. However, this approach was found to be less effective than the application of a deep convolutional network. The incorporation of a geolocation module has the potential to benefit real-world applications by making the model more adaptable and robust. Furthermore, the researchers suggested that incorporating the camera's field of view and the weather conditions' effects on the image's color and texture could further enhance the accuracy of weather classification in aerial images. Our analysis examines how climate change interest shifts among diverse groups and how their individual interests interconnect. Initially, we track the individual trends, followed by developing a cross-influence model that we then validate using a VAR model. Our results indicate significant fluctuations in the general public's climate change interest, as evident from our creation of a Climate Change Index for Europe and the US based on media mentions, whereas economists show relatively little interest as measured by prominent journal publications. Interestingly, science journals and policymakers display a more stable interest in the subject, albeit with policymakers typically becoming interested somewhat later. Furthermore, our analysis suggests that science's climate change focus is closely aligned with the overall public's interest, while policymakers' interest is more closely tied to economic considerations. Ultimately, our model reveals a complex system where changes in one group's interest may not directly influence another, but rather, understanding these dynamics is essential to making accurate predictions. Our findings are particularly relevant to practitioners seeking to influence public discourse on climate change and highlight the significance of considering multiple stakeholders' interests when developing strategies to shape the relevant social norm. Finally, our analysis provides a useful framework for studying the interactions of various social norms, offering a versatile approach that could be applied to a broad range of topics and differentiator groups. Soft grippers are increasingly popular in robotics due to their distinct advantages, 
including the ability to adapt to varying environments and objects. However, their 
movement and grasping are heavily influenced by unpredictable fluid dynamics, 
making it challenging to model them accurately. Most soft gripper control methods 
involve using finite element models or empirical approximations, but these can be 
time-consuming to set up and may not account for unexpected situations. This work 
introduces a novel control method that utilizes the Koopman operator theory to model 
and regulate soft grippers online. By integrating periodic motion estimation and 
the spectral decomposition of a Koopman operator, this approach can learn from 
experiments and generate predictive models for gripper behavior. These models 
can then be used for linear control design, enabling swift adaptation to changing 
situations. Our method was successfully tested on a soft gripper in a laboratory 
setting, and we found that it can generate accurate models and effective control 
strategies rapidly. Furthermore, we discovered that our method can transfer 
knowledge from one gripper configuration to another, which is essential for the 
grasping and manipulation of complex objects. The benefits of this approach were 
demonstrated in a series of video demonstrations available online. Our method 
significantly reduces the online feedback control costs associated with soft 
grinders, while also eliminating the need for complex and time-consuming finite 
element modeling. As a result, we believe that our method has the potential to 
revolutionize the movement and manipulation of soft grippers. The code for our

A new study reveals that gravitational wave memory emissions could contribute a substantial portion of the gravitational wave background, potentially exceeding the threshold for detection by LIGO's third observing run. The source's amplitude is influenced by the rate at which black holes and neutron stars merge, resulting in a stochastic gravitational wave background with a characteristic frequency range of approximately 0.1 to 100 Hz. Specifically, the amplitude of this gravitational wave memory signal is on the order of $10^{-21}-10^{-18} \text{str} \text{Hz}^{-1}\,,$ which is comparable to, yet slightly higher than, the binary blackhole gravitational wave background in the same frequency range. Consequently, the gravitational wave memory background may pose a significant challenge for LIGO's third observing run, potentially making it harder to detect binary black-hole gravitational waves. Conversely, the gravitational wave memory background could greatly enhance the LIGO-Virgo detector network's ability to detect gravitational waves from binary black hole mergers during their O3 run, if the detectors are able to effectively mitigate or remove the gravitational wave memory signal. Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints in real-world applications. This study introduces decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, allowing a model to be trained on the behavior of a network whose internal workings are inaccessible, as long as it produces classification outputs. When access to the original data is possible, a training sample's contribution to the distillation loss is split into two parts: one that relies on the network's decision, and another that uses the actual input, with the latter acting as a traditional knowledge distillation loss. When decision-based distillation is the only option, the loss is solely based on the network's decision, with the model's behavior being evaluated against that decision rather than the original input. Notably, our method doesn't require the original network to be part of the training process, instead relying on query-based evaluation to gauge the network's response to specific data points. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through experiments involving various network architectures, such as ResNet, MobileNet, and SeNet, across the ImageNet dataset. Our method achieves significant improvements, with certain models seeing a 4.5% top-1 error reduction and 5.3% error rate reduction compared to the default distillation method. The code and models have been made publicly available. Additionally, our method has a reduced computational cost, with training times under 3 minutes for models with more than 5 million parameters when using the decision-based distillation loss. We show that certain models trained using our method can match the performance of networks with twice to three times the number of parameters. Our method has potential applications in various domains, such as network compression, where the original network may be part of a distributed computing system or is otherwise inaccessible. Similarly, it could be employed in scenarios where the original network needs to be stored or is readily available through an API, among other scenarios. This project tackles the complex problem of simultaneously monitoring the positions and shapes of hands and objects in a sequence of depth point cloud data, starting from the known poses in the initial frame. To achieve this, we introduce a network called HandTrackNet, the first point cloud-based hand joint tracking system, to calculate hand joint movement between frames. Our novel hand pose canonicalization approach simplifies this task and enables accurate tracking of hand joints. By analyzing these joints, we reconstruct the original 3D hand and object interactions, which are essential for many applications like gesture language learning and object grasping. To evaluate the effectiveness of HandTrackNet, we created a diverse and challenging dataset called the Hand Object Interaction Dataset (HOID), containing 20 common household objects and various gestures. Our dataset features 80,000 depth images, accompanied by ground truth information on hand and object shapes, positions, and movements. Handpose-CNN, a state-of-the-art hand pose estimation network, is modified to generate the required ground truth for this task. To validate HandTrackNet, we conducted numerous experiments using different sequences and viewpoints, and our results show that it outperforms other methods, including those using RGB images, by accurately tracking the positions and shapes of hands and objects in a sequence of depth point cloud data. A collaborative robot (collab robot) is designed to work seamlessly with human staff by simplifying complex manufacturing tasks. To achieve this, the collab robot must accurately pinpoint the position of its end-effector in relation to the human. However, dependence on an optical camera for tracking is problematic due to potential interference from surrounding objects and the added expense. Our proposed solution involves using a depth sensor in tandem with the camera to develop a method for calibrating the robot's vision system without relying on a dedicated calibration device. Our algorithm achieves this by using a mathematical algorithm derived from maximum likelihood principles on a specific dataset, allowing us to estimate the position of the end-effector's optical, depth, and pose projections. Our experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed method in a simulated 3D environment and two real-world scenarios. Our code has been made publicly available on a specified GitHub repository. Additionally, two video recordings documenting our research have been uploaded to the specified YouTube channel. Our method shows promising results, with estimated pose accuracy rates of 97% for a 6D estimation method and 99% for a 3D estimation method, respectively. These accuracy rates far surpass those of existing state-of-the-art methods. Moreover, our approach boasts a significant time-saving advantage, with processing times of approximately 10 milliseonds for a 6D estimation method and 6 milliseonds for a 3D estimation method, respectively. These processing times are remarkably swift, with our approach outperforming existing methods by a substantial margin. Our method not only relies heavily on the use of depth data but also incorporates several innovative features, including the incorporation of uncertainty data, the use of non-linear optimization algorithms, and the application of specific regularization techniques to enhance its performance. Furthermore, our approach is versatile, with our methods applicable to a wide range of end-effector designs, including cylindrical-shaped end-effectors, regardless of their specific geometry. To validate our methods, we conducted experiments using two publicly available datasets and two custom-built datasets, with our results demonstrating a notable improvement in performance over existing state-of-the-art methods. Our approach not only outperforms existing methods but also showcases its versatility, with our results applicable to a wide range of applications beyond simple object tracking. Specifically, we believe our research will have a significant impact on various tasks, including object manipulation, human-robot collaboration, and more broadly, across various fields such as manufacturing, healthcare, and social robotics. Our research provides a valuable contribution to these areas by facilitating enhanced collaboration between humans

A new model is introduced to describe treatment interference in units, 
where the response is influenced solely by its treatment status and neighboring units within a defined radius of influence (K-neighborhood). Traditional approaches for identifying treatment interference compare the responses of treated and control units with and without connections to treated units. In this research, a more comprehensive framework is developed to assess the validity of this approach and detect treatment interference within a specified K-neighborhood. A test is proposed that does so without requiring knowledge of the underlying interference model, supporting consistent estimates of the test's asymptotic behavior. Conditions are established for the test's effectiveness in various experimental settings, including those with network structures and limited observational data. When the data follow a linear model, a simpler test is introduced with stronger asymptotic results. Through simulations, the finite-sample performance of the tests is evaluated, revealing that the proposed tests can accurately identify treatment interference even in small sample sizes. In an empirical analysis of a medical device's effects on a graph of patient relationships, the methods demonstrate the detection of treatment interference among closely related patients. Additionally, a test is introduced for detecting the presence of treatment effects. Both tests show strong performance in the given examples and have been made available in the R package 'DetectTI'. A detailed outline of the approach, along with the software and associated data, is provided at a dedicated website. Previous research has suggested the use of SRAM-based TRNGs for extracting entropy from SRAM arrays. As these arrays are commonly used for data storage, their built-in redundancy could potentially be utilized for generating random numbers. However, existing SRAM-based TRNGs have several drawbacks, including high energy consumption, prolonged latency, and limited flexibility. To address these limitations, this study proposes an SRAM-based TRNG that can operate at any desired rate. To achieve this, the SRAM array is subjected to reduced supply voltage, causing adjacent bits to become disordered due to the increased bit-line capacitance. The extracted bits are then filtered through a parity-based scheme to produce high-quality random numbers. The proposed design exhibits several advantages over existing SRAM-based TRNGs, including its ability to generate random numbers at various rates, extract entropy from a large SRAM array, and operate with a wide range of supply voltages. Moreover, it outperforms existing TRNGs in terms of randomness quality, and significantly reduces energy consumption and computational complexity compared to other SRAM-based TRNGs. The results of extensive simulations verify the efficacy of the proposed design. For example, when tested with a 40nm SRAM array, the proposed design demonstrated high randomness quality, a low kullback-leibler distance of 0.18, and a high mutual information capacity of 0.95. Additionally, the design exhibited energy efficiency, a high entropy rate of 0.97, and a relatively short period of 2048, outperforming alternative SRNGs in nearly all aspects. Furthermore, the design exhibits scalability, and its performance with a 28nm SRAM array was also evaluated. The results showed that the SRAM-based TRNG with undervolting exhibits superior performance and quality compared to traditional SRAM-based TRNGs. Based on these findings, the proposed design, named TuRaN, can serve as a reliable and efficient solution for generating random numbers. The design will be made available upon request. The source code can be accessed at the following repository: https://github.com/abdullahalowais/SRAM-based_TRNG. Additionally, the design can be accessed through the following link: https://hdl.bitbucket.org/ucsb-edu/edu_ucsb_ece_162_f2020_lecture20_sram_based_trng. We explore the behavior of photon-photon interactions in a $q$-deformed optomechanical system, where both the optomechanical field and the mechanical field are represented by $q$-oscillators. Automated essay grading has been a persistent challenge in Natural Language Processing.  Despite years of research, it remains only partially implemented in practice, primarily due to difficulties in adapting models to different educational settings and content requirements.  A significant obstacle to progress is likely the lack of accessible, high-quality data for training and fine-tuning advanced NLP models.  In this research, we explore the potential of data augmentation techniques to enhance the performance of state-of-the-art transformer-based automated essay grading models when working with limited and imperfect training data.  A combination of approaches, including back-translation, word replacement, and sentence replication, is applied to two datasets of different sizes.  Our results, however, did not consistently support the efficacy of data augmentation in this specific context.  Instead, we discovered that the suitability of data augmentation methods depends on the characteristics and complexity of the target text domain.  Building on these findings, we suggest that data augmentation may not necessarily improve performance when applied to complex tasks like automated essay grading.  In contrast, it could potentially harm performance if not carefully implemented or applied to texts that are already overly simplistic.  To inform future research on data augmentation, we provide a detailed analysis of the effects produced by different methods on the chosen datasets and offer a more nuanced understanding of the relationships between text attributes and the efficacy of data augmentation techniques.  Ultimately, our study concludes with preliminary observations on the challenges and limitations of data augmentation in NLP tasks involving informal texts, such as student essays.  In particular, we note that the scarcity of labeled data remains a significant obstacle to progress in this area, a problem compounded by the particularities of our chosen dataset.  In addition, we highlight the need for more systematic evaluations of data augmentation methods that take into account the specific characteristics of the target domain, rather than relying on performance metrics alone.  In the spirit of this challenge, we make our augmented datasets available for other researchers to build upon.

We propose an upgraded RingCT protocol that incorporates a delegation mechanism, allowing users to transfer RingCT's anonymity features to other transactions. This delegation can occur through a straightforward process that doesn't compromise anonymity when combined with standard RingCT transactions. The main advantage of our Delegated RingCT (DRCT) protocol is a significant reduction in transaction size, resulting in lower mineral fee costs for participants in the mixing process. By minimizing the size of transactions, DRCT increases the number of transactions that can be processed within a single mixing cycle, making the protocol more efficient and scalable. Comprehensive security analyses, including memory and computation attacks, as well as an investigation of transaction size, reveal that DRCT maintains the same level of anonymity benefits with reduced costs. The performance gains of DRCT are demonstrated through real-world transaction examples, showcasing the improved efficiency of our protocol. Furthermore, an economic analysis highlights the potential for increased revenue among DRCT participants due to lower transaction costs. The proposed DRCT protocol is currently being implemented in the Zclassic and Zcash nodes. Research is ongoing to further optimize the protocol and evaluate its results. Previous Hebrew NLP initiatives relied on outdated, scanned text versions from the 19th and early 20th centuries. To address the lack of modern, treebanked data, we have developed IsrTreebank, a comprehensive bank of written texts since 1948. IsrTreebank covers various topics including news articles from Haaretz, product descriptions, and user-generated content. The bank's corpus is open-source at https://github.com/HebrewNLP/IsrTreebank. We have created 10,000 annotated sentences so far and plan to add more in the future. In this study, we present our annotation guidelines and present new parsing results for Hebrew, achieving a 94.4% F1 score on CoNLL Shared Task 2019's metrics. We also discuss the challenges of annotating modern Hebrew, a language that has undergone significant changes in its writing system and vocabulary since 1948. Notably, the increased use of acronyms and Hebrew and English mixed text poses new challenges for NLP. The project's goals extend beyond enhancing NLP models to include the preservation of historical texts for future generations. In particular, we have developed methods to easily convert our corpus into timelines, enabling researchers to explore significant events like the Six-Day War and the Yom Kippur War alongside corresponding changes in language usage. We have found that NLP models perform better on texts from periods we have insufficient annotated data for, and that our annotated data can in turn improve the quality of Wikipedia articles on these topics. Thus, this project offers a unique fusion of NLP and preservation efforts. We have also discovered that our bank's value extends beyond Hebrew NLP alone, as it can serve as a resource for general NLP research due to its diverse topics and the broad range of words it includes. The bank's words are evenly distributed between words that appear once and those that appear 10,000 times or more, offering a unique dataset for NLP analysis. An advanced modular system, which is known as the safety filter, has been designed to enhance potentially unsafe control inputs with safety assurances through constraint satisfaction. This paper presents a refined model predictive safety filter (MPSF) that utilizes system level synthesis techniques to create an expanded safety area for linear systems impacted by bounded disturbances. The resulting SL-MPSF method ensures system safety with fewer and less extreme adjustments to control inputs. Furthermore, we propose a specific variant of SL-MPSF that retains scalability and significantly decreases online processing requirements, which is the major drawback of traditional MPSF designs. The benefits of our safety filter design over state-of-the-art MPSF designs are demonstrated through numerical examples. Additionally, we provide software tools that enable the creation of expanded safety areas for certain safety problems. These tools are based on the MATLAB programming language and are named SLSAFETY and MPSF_TOOL, respectively. Both of these tools is available for public use at https://github.com/AA-LAB/SLSAFETY. Also, the associated data is available at https://doi.org/10.6084/m1FWSE-0000Q-0000.

Our research aims to examine the impact of varying training corpora on this learning approach. We discover that models trained on informal data perform notably better on downstream tasks within the same context, in comparison to those trained on more formal datasets. Moreover, by analyzing the behavior of these models, we find that they are able to learn in-context more effectively due to the richer implicit knowledge present in informal corpora, which enables better generalization. Our findings indicate that models trained on informal data tend to exhibit superior in-context learning capabilities. Interestingly, while models trained on formal data may demonstrate higher single-token accuracy, this difference does not translate to in-context learning advantages. Our study provides valuable insights for those seeking to enhance in-context learning by leveraging models trained on informal data. Additionally, it also suggests that there is a need to explore more diverse training corpora to unlock the full potential of this learning approach. Galaxy cluster observations have consistently shown the presence of intracluster medium (ICM), revealing the intricate processes governing the evolution of these massive systems. The ICM's behavior is influenced by various physical phenomena, including thermal conduction, magnetic fields, and radiation. Our two-dimensional simulations of galaxy cluster core formation investigated the effects of thermal conduction, magnetic fields, and radiative cooling. We discovered that the ICM's behavior significantly depends on the strength of these processes. When thermal conduction is high, it prevents the formation of dense, cooling clouds. Magnetic fields, on the other hand, facilitate the growth of such clouds by creating a unstable, magnetized fluid that accumulates near the cluster's center. The growth of these cooling clouds is further enhanced when the plasma beta value is low, as it allows the magnetic field to dominate the fluid's behavior. Furthermore, our simulations demonstrated the formation of small, unstable, cooling structures in addition to large, visible cooling clouds. The presence of these small structures may contribute to an enhanced cooling rate within the ICM, as they create an intricate network that increases the ICM's surface area. Our results provide valuable insights for future galaxy cluster simulations and observations, potentially leading to a more in-depth understanding of the ICM's behavior and the evolution of these massive astrophysical systems. Additionally, we propose an alternative method for simulating galaxy cluster core formation, as our findings may be applicable to other massive cluster systems. The growth of cooling clouds could also be beneficial for high-speed radio jets, as they could provide essential nutrients for the growth of radio galaxies. The growth of these cooling structures may also play a role in the formation of star-forming or star-forming quiescent galaxies through the regulation of the ICM by high-speed jets. A new scientific approach called the basket trial is emerging, which involves studying multiple patient subsets simultaneously to develop targeted treatments. One key issue with basket trials is calculating the required sample size, which can be complex due to the reliance on event rates from other patient subsets for statistical inference. Our study develops methods for determining the necessary sample size in basket trials that allow information sharing between subsets. We consider two scenarios: one where the subpopulations' treatment effects are the same, and another where their effects differ. Our methods use Bayesian principles and are illustrated with two examples. The first example involves a binary endpoint in a basket trial with four subsets, while the second example examines a continuous endpoint in a basket trial with eight subsets. Both examples highlight the importance of carefully selecting which subsets can share information and the desired level of information sharing. Our methods enable more efficient sample size calculations, allowing for larger trials with available resources or earlier go-no-go decisions. Specifically, increasing the level of information sharing from none to moderate can significantly reduce the required sample size by as much as 50%. Our methods are available on R through the SiBiBayes package. We advocate for further research to develop methods that can accurately model the diverse patient subsets and to investigate the trade-offs between faster go-no-go decisions and potential losses in detecting subset-specific effects. We also suggest exploring alternative Bayesian approaches, such as using prior distributions based on historical data or through the BioShiny platform which allows users to create and deploy Bayesian analyses for clinical trials. Finally, we outline future research directions, such as extending our methods to assess the impact of shared information on Type I and II error rates. We use simulations to compare the performance of our sample size methods with classical approaches, demonstrating that Bayesian sharing can reduce the required sample size without compromising statistical power. To satisfy the rising demands of high-throughput in the industry, advanced motion systems must now exhibit two key characteristics: high-speed and high-precision. The variety of systems one can systemize under this requirement encompasses automated telescopes, spacecraft positioning and atomic force microscopes, among others. The changes in some of these systems' parameters with time can be considered as slow-varying parameters (SVPs), while others have parameters that fluctuate rapidly. The use of the linear parameter-varying (LPV) feedback framework has been shown to effectively improve the performance of motion control systems affected by time-varying parameters. This study presents an LPV-based sequential loop closing (SLC) strategy, aiming to reduce the impact of rapid SVP changes on the performance of motion control systems. The proposed SLC algorithm determines the optimal sampling instant for feedback signal updating based on the current state of the system's parameter, using an LPV feedback controller. The effectiveness of the LPV SLC strategy was evaluated in simulation using two case studies: a linear system with a single SVP and a nonlinear system with two SVPs. Segmentation of anatomical structures in medical images is a critical process for further procedures such as surgery and tissue removal. While fully automated segmentation methods exist, they are often limited to images from the same modality as the training data. To address this, we've developed a novel approach, called cyclic segmentation GAN, that allows for multi-modality instance segmentation without relying on ground truth labels during training. Our method consists of two generators and two discriminators working in tandem to segment images from different imaging modalities. Through experiments on MRI-CT prostate segmentation, we've found that our approach outperforms existing methods, achieving a Dice score of 0.755, 0.624, and 0.574 for the MRI, CT, and combined modalities respectively. Notably, this method performs better than a technique that uses fully supervised ground truth labels, underscoring its effectiveness. Our proposed approach enables more flexible and generalizable segmentation, ultimately facilitating easier clinical applications. inferring accurate and missing event and temporal knowledge graph information.
Building upon successful applications of tensor decomposition in static graph
completions, we introduce Time-LowFER - an extension of the low-rank factorization
model that is both efficient in parameters and attentive to time constraints.
We recognize current time representation approaches' shortcomings and suggest a
cycle-aware time-encoding framework to enhance time understanding and model
generalizability. Our unified framework can be integrated with numerous existing KGC
models. Experimental results demonstrate the benefits of our proposed framework,
as it surpasses state-of-the-art performance in the evaluation of temporal knowledge
graph completions. Moreover, our model is both scalable and suitable for large
datasets. The source code is available at https://github.com/whaiwhai/Time_LowFER.

In simulated sound environments, the sound produced by movements on the ground (ground sound) is often overlooked, as sound sources and agents' positions are typically presented in mid-air. This paper investigates the importance of ground sound in 3D audio simulation. Our analysis reveals that ground sound is a significant component of sound simulation, particularly in first-person games and applications where player perspective is applied to camera and audio. Additionally, we identify four practical applications of ground sound and discuss two methods for simulating it, considering both theoretical and practical implications. While a detailed theory of ground sound exists, its practical application within sound simulation remains unexplored. Our aim is to encourage the use of ground sound in practical sound simulation scenarios. Experimental examples, including a demo with VR capabilities, can be found on our website at https://graphics.unimontelab.org/sound-on-ground/.

A prevalent form of demonstrating Bell nonlocality known as the Bell inequality theorem has been the cornerstone of Bell inequality experiments for decades. However, the recognition that certain events in quantum physics have lower probabilities than expected by the Bell inequality has led to the development of more stringent criteria, such as the nonexistence of local hidden variables and the violation of the Bell inequality, even in the presence of random noise. We have successfully fulfilled this more rigorous standard in an experiment, achieving the violation of the Bell inequality without exhibiting clear inequalities, instead relying on specific quantum correlations. Our experiment, conducted using projective measurements on polarized photons, showed a Bell violation of 0.176, significantly larger than the expected inequality violation of 0.053. This outcome has implications for the development of quantum communication protocols, particularly when realistic noise is present, and has enabled us to estimate the minimum noise level required for the violation of the Bell inequality to prevail. Our results have further indicated that the violation of the Bell inequality and the existence of quantum entanglement are two distinct phenomena. We have also explored various measurement methods and found that both sharp and unsharp measurements can be employed to violate the Bell inequality. We have analyzed the relationship between the widths of measured states and the violation of the Bell inequality, and identified a critical width below which the violation of the Bell inequality is no longer possible. This critical width has been found to be dependent on the specific quantum state used in the experiment and the specific Bell inequality under consideration. We have also estimated the maximum width of the measured states for which the violation of the Bell inequality remains significant, and found this value to be compatible with the widths of commonly used mesodescriptors. We have further examined the influence of noise on the violation of the Bell inequality and found that while broad distributions of noise may obscure the violation of the Bell inequality, a precise estimation of noise can reveal its presence. We have demonstrated that the violation of the Bell inequality is a robust quantum property, and even in the presence of random noise, it remains distinct from the corresponding probabilities predicted by local hidden variables. Furthermore, we have shown that the violation of the Bell inequality can be achieved not only with sharp, well-defined measurement outcomes, but also with wider mesodescriptors, and that the violation of the Bell inequality is a reliable indicator of quantum entanglement, and can be utilized in the development of reliable quantum communication protocols. We establish that for a locally free Noetherian algebra R, having either a countable basis or an infinite set of linearly independent elements implies the existence of an R-algebra with a specific property: specific linear operators over that algebra are surjective, yet the algebra itself is not divisible. This conclusion holds even in the absence of commutativity. Furthermore, we demonstrate that for a locally free Noetherian commutative algebra, having either a countable basis or an infinite set of linearly independent elements implies the existence of polynomials with specific properties such that the algebra itself is not divisible for those polynomials, yet the operators are surjective. This line of reasoning does not apply to algebra R itself, however. On the other hand, we show that for a free commutative algebra, having either a countable basis or an infinite set of linearly independent elements results in all linear operators being surjective. Finally, we explore whether our findings could be generalized to more complex linear algebra configurations. In contrast to current methods, introducing non-linear techniques may hold the key to further breakthroughs in this field. Lastly, we examine the relationship between our conclusions and the Freiheitssatz for Artinian algebras, identifying both similarities and differences between these theorems. Additionally, we propose several open questions for further study.

This paper revisits monitoring real-time systems by leveraging properties described either in Metric Interval Temporal Logic or as Timed B\"uchi Automata. We propose effective, symbolic, and online monitoring methods in several contexts that take advantage of 'zones', a concept familiar from efficient model checking of Timed Automata. These contexts encompass improved treatment of timing discrepancies, monitoring under timing ambiguity, and the extension of monitoring to provide earliest time estimates for when decisive verdicts can be rendered. This last aspect is also known as'monitoring with horizon' or'recursion depth'. Our work builds upon previous studies, combining them and adding new insights that yield similar, albeit sometimes simplified, complexity results. Additionally, we present an implementation of our monitoring methods and illustrate their utility with a practical example involving scheduled task management in the Linux kernel. This example showcases the benefits of'monitoring with horizon' in reducing monitoring complexity under timing inaccuracies. Furthermore, the example highlights a timing-related incompatibility between the Linux kernel's interaction with modern CPUs and our developed formal framework. This incompatibility is attributed to the kernel's usage of timer intervals that are twice as long as those used by the CPU, resulting in the kernel's behavior falling outside of our defined temporal logic and requiring'monitoring with horizon' for proper compliance analysis. Finally, we outline possible solutions to mitigate this incompatibility, thereby enhancing the applicability of our monitoring methods to real-time embedded systems such as the Linux kernel. These solutions involve rounding the kernel's timer values either to the nearest multiple of 1us or to the actual hardware values, both of which would result in falling within our defined temporal logic and making the kernel behavior eligible for our monitoring methods. This incompatibility and potential solutions have been verified through a practical monitoring and verification process involving the Linux kernel's task management code. This code has been successfully checked using our developed online monitoring method, and the results have been documented in a configurable format suitable for further analysis. This analysis has revealed that rounding either to the nearest multiple of 1us or to the actual hardware values would facilitate the efficient and symbolic monitoring of the Linux kernel's real-time behavior using our developed formal framework. This has significant practical implications and has been thoroughly verified, thereby substantiating the potential benefits of our monitoring methods in real-world embedded systems such as the Linux kernel. Our analysis incorporates the vector-meson dominance model and utilizes a finite-range interaction. Our findings reveal that, in the presence of an imbalance in chiral charges, the mass spectrum of vector mesons undergoes modifications. Specifically, the masses of $\rho$ and $\omega$ mesons increase, whereas that of $\phi$ meson remains unaltered. Moreover, as the magnitude of chiral imbalance $(\mu)$ grows, the mass of vector mesons exhibits a greater dependence on the vector meson's momentum than on its mass itself. In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter configurations, solving the constraint equations may become unfeasible due to the intricate nature of the system. Our novel approach, called CTTK, enables researchers to bypass the constraint equations, thus avoiding the associated difficulties and limitations. Similar to the conventional Conformal Transverse Traceless method, CTTK utilizes a conformal transformation to eliminate the mean conformal field, but unlike its predecessor, CTTK does not require solving the constraint equations for the conformal field. Instead, we rely on a crude approximation that is sufficient for a second-order solution. Our methodology produces a second-order accurate mean conformal field, which, combined with the techniques of "projection" and "transport", enables researchers to achieve a highly accurate solution. Our work demonstrates that the CTTK method is particularly effective in challenging scenarios where the average conformal field is heavily influenced by random or short-wavelength perturbations. Additionally, we show that the CTTK method leads to a substantial reduction in computational time required to generate initial data configurations. Specifically, we found that the runtime is approximately 10 times shorter than what's required for the standard TTK method. Our findings are substantiated through various numerical tests, including those involving the resolution of 768^3 grid cells and a wide range of perturbation amplitudes. Overall, the CTTK method represents a groundbreaking advancement in the development of initial data configurations for numerical relativity, especially when dealing with intricate matter configurations. Our work is expected to have a significant impact on researchers working on simulating black-hole binary initial data, as well as those studying the growth of short-wave-length perturbations. Our code, named cttk, has been thoroughly tested and is publicly available at https://github.com/ianclarkphd/cttk. Furthermore, we have prepared a comprehensive guide to implementing the CTTK method, which can be found at https://ianclarkphd.github.io/cttk. We eagerly anticipate the method's adoption by the numerical relativity community.

The main objective of the JUNO experiment involves measuring the neutrino mass hierarchy by observing the neutrino mass ordering in a large underground detector. To achieve this goal, the experiment requires a massive photomultiplier tube system consisting of over 20,000 individual 20-inch PMTs that provide accurate coverage of the active volume. For the successful implementation of the experiment, it is crucial to ensure the quality of these PMTs by thoroughly testing and evaluating their performance under real-world conditions. A comprehensive testing process involving a detailed examination of the PMTs has been developed and implemented. This process consists of a series of tests that evaluate the PMTs based on their optical, electrical, and physical properties. A significant aspect of this process involves the mass testing phase where a large number of PMTs are tested in a large underground water tank to simulate real-world operational conditions. To support the large-scale PMT testing program, the development of advanced testing equipment and the creation of a sophisticated PMT testing system were necessary. In this paper, the mass testing equipment, the testing system, and the results of the PMTs' optical and electrical properties as well as their overall quality are presented. Additionally, the details of the two main stages of the testing process and the criteria used to evaluate the PMTs' quality are explained in detail. The results of the tests, including the combined scores based on the PMTs' overall performance, are presented and discussed. The outcome of the testing program indicates that the majority of the 20-inch PMTs meet the required standards and are suitable for use in the JUNO experiment. However, a small percentage of the PMTs do not meet the required standards and must be replaced with new ones. The reasons behind the non-compliant PMTs as well as the replacement process are presented and explained in detail. The testing program's outcomes and the details of the work undertaken to ensure the quality of the JUNO's large-scale detector components are documented. The success of the testing program will serve as a model and reference for future similar large-scale detector projects. The information and knowledge gained from this project can be applied to other projects as an example of best practice. Astronomical observations from space or near space are often impeded by the distorted light passing through the Earth's atmosphere due to varying refractive index across different spectral domains. The difference in refractive index can cause a phenomenon known as atmospheric dispersion that distorts the light and limits long baseline telescopes' effectiveness. In order to correct this, the design of SPIDER, a stratospheric balloon experiment, incorporates a pupil-plane filter to minimize the effects of atmospheric dispersion. The implementation of this filter relies on an accurate model of the atmosphere's behavior. However, since there are various atmospheric models that can be utilized, it is necessary to establish a relationship between these models and the observed results to ensure the accuracy of the correction process. This study uses observed data from three distinct sources - the transfer function of the atmosphere, the phase structure function, and the spectral energy distribution of the atmosphere - to compare different atmospheric models. Formulas that enable the comparison of these models to the observed data are developed, and the results from multiple atmospheric models are analyzed. Ultimately, a measure of how well each model fits the observed data is used to characterize and compare the accuracy of various atmospheric models for different atmospheric conditions. The relationship between these model characterization tools and the observed data is investigated, and the time it takes for the atmosphere to change significantly, known as the timescale of variability, is identified. The study finds that the time it takes for the atmosphere to change is typically around 30 minutes or less, and the observed data is compared to the results from a different study on the subject. The study concludes by providing a way to quickly and efficiently compare the accuracy of different atmospheric models for specific observing conditions, and paves the way for a more comprehensive comparison between the observed data and the results from a stratospheric balloon experiment. The relationship between the model characterization and the observed results is further investigated in a companion paper. We introduce PILE, an effective method for supervising multi-teacher distillation using student-network-based logits. This approach iteratively trains teachers using feedback from the student, which is represented by logits. PILE can be viewed as combining two techniques: feedback-based teacher training and logits-based correction. By employing the student to guide the teachers, PILE optimizes each teacher more effectively and mitigates discrepancies between the teachers and the student, ultimately resulting in improved knowledge distillation. Our experimental findings demonstrate that PILE achieves superior distillation outcomes on various models, outperforming current methods across multiple benchmarks. Moreover, PILE's convergence speed far exceeds that of alternative methods, with our experiments showing that PILE can achieve superior results after just two iterations. When applied to a 3-layer ResNet34 model on the ImageNet dataset, PILE exhibited a remarkable 6.7% error reduction compared to the baseline, with our best-performing configuration achieving a comparable error rate to that of the large teacher model. This paper explores the recovery of one-dimensional functions from measurements, focusing on sparse vector spaces and continuous domains like the interval $[0,1]$. Under specific conditions, including bounded variation within a chosen metric and a prescribed threshold for the norm of the recovery matrix, we establish that the solution to the basis pursuit problem is unique and derive a convergence rate for an iterative method, such as the gradient descent. regions in frames and temporal segments through its multi-step attention mechanism.
Evaluations of the model on established action recognition benchmarks indicate
remarkable performance superiority. For instance, on HMDB51, HAN surpasses the
competition by 4.5% and 7.8% in terms of accuracy, respectively, when compared 
to VGG-16 and ResNet-50 models. Similarly, on UCF101, HAN exhibits improved 
accuracy of 3.2% and 5.9% over the aforementioned models. Consequently, HAN

A highly nonlinear equation results in a challenging system for multiple reasons, including the fact that existing solutions deteriorate over time, the lack of a clear boundary condition, and the possibility of vanishing densities. To improve the overall system, we introduce a new notion of solution and show that it yields a single, enduring solution. To establish the existence of this new solution, we devise a diagonalization method that allows us to combine several techniques. Along the way, we develop a series of auxiliary lemmas, including ones that address a generalization of the Birkhoff Recurrent Theorem and the creation of a blow-up boundary layer. To strengthen our new notion of solution, we apply several mathematical theorems, including L^p inequalities, the Holder inequality, and the measure theory. A significant outcome of our work is the discovery that the general measure-valued solution of the conservation law can be expressed as the sum of a bounded $L^1$ function and a dissipation term that decreases over time. To illustrate the complexity of our new notion of solution, we provide several examples, including ones that demonstrate the creation of a singularity, a multiple-interaction scenario, and a solution with a boundary layer. Finally, we show that our new notion of solution satisfies a fundamental property known as the entropy condition. This movement can significantly impact ecosystems as animals interact with each other and their surroundings. To study these interactions, biologists need to automatically detect animal locomotion in video footage over large areas, such as entire ecosystems. To address this issue, we propose a new method that uses deep learning to identify animal locomotion in videos. Our approach relies on a vast video dataset of marine life to learn the characteristics of biological movement. This method not only saves human effort by automating the process but also provides more accurate results than current state-of-the-art models. Additionally, we outline possible extensions to this research, including the development of domain-specific models for different environments and the exploration of multiple modalities such as acoustic data. These potential directions are discussed in more detail in the accompanying paper. Optimizing power networks involves finding the most cost-effective way to distribute power and meet customer demand. This goal can be achieved by identifying the optimal configuration of power flow lines, but the numerous variables and constraints associated with the problem make it computationally challenging. In fact, it's one of the most intractable combinatorial optimization problems, rendering classical solutions often impractical or approximate. To address this issue, the proposed study leverages the capabilities of quantum computing to create more effective solutions. By incorporating a hybrid quantum-classical approach utilizing the QAOA algorithm, the researchers introduce a novel circuit design that yields substantial improvements. Specifically, the results indicate that the hybrid circuit surpasses the performance of the classical branch and cut method, while also outperforming a comparative quantum-only approach. Moreover, the hybrid circuit's performance is enhanced when the problem is split into smaller sub-problems. The researchers also examine the impact of noise on the quantum circuit and propose future research avenues to further mitigate this influence. Overall, the study showcases the potential of quantum computing to tackle complex optimization issues, particularly those in power networks. Furthermore, the proposed circuits can be adapted to address various other optimization challenges. Lastly, the researchers highlight that future quantum computing noise can be circumvented with sufficient scaling, underscoring the long-term promise of quantum computing in optimizing power networks. To that end, the proposed circuits will be made publicly available to enable other researchers to replicate the results and build upon the approaches. The detailed source code can be accessed at a designated URL. Additionally, the researchers introduce two new methods to tackle the optimization problem, which have been patented and will soon be published in greater detail. The quantum circuits, describing the optimal solutions to the power network optimization problem, will also be made accessible on the quantum computing cloud platform, IARPA's RECKON project, for other researchers to access and utilize.
