The Stable Roommates problem involves matching a set of agents with items, ensuring that the resulting matches remain stable when any two agents swap partners, preferring each other over their current counterparts. A general approach to finding stable matches employs the concept of valuations, allowing agents to rank items in order of preference. The additive stable roommates problem (ASRP) offers a valuation structure where an agent's preference is the sum of individual components, each corresponding to a particular item. We examine the three-dimensional version of ASRP where each agent can possess up to three items. Notably, we prove that finding stable matches in 3D-ASRP may become computationally complex when the number of available items exceeds the number of agents. Nonetheless, we develop an efficient algorithm to find stable matches in 3D-ASRP with a linear number of calculations, regardless of the number of items. Our approach builds upon a linear-time algorithm designed for two-dimensional ASRP, allowing each agent to possess a maximum of two items. A key concept in our solution involves the application of 'good' sets, which help agents eliminate impractical match options, ultimately leading to a stable match. Additionally, we define a new notion of 'indivisibility' for agent preferences and demonstrate that requiring each agent to be indivisible in the 3D-ASRP setting makes finding stable matches a solvable problem, even for large numbers of items. Finally, we explore the relationship between the number of agents and the number of items required to guarantee the existence of at least one stable match. Our investigation involves the application of the probabilistic method to find suitable configurations of agents and items. A particular challenge arises in the 3D-ASRP when there are more agents than items since it becomes uncertain whether stable matches even exist in such situations, even with the requirement that each agent should be indivisible. Leveraging the concept of 'good' sets once more, we prove a novel result about the minimum number of agents needed, given a fixed number of items. Our work culminates in a comprehensive examination of the additive stable roommates problem with general, additive preferences for any number of dimensions. The results presented can be applied to a broader range of settings, including the recently introduced multi-dimensional stable marriage problem. Moreover, our research offers insights into using additively separable preferences in a stable marriage or roommates setting with more than two dimensions. Ultimately, our results shed light on the properties of additive preference structures and their impact on finding stable matches in various configuration settings.

Large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing relies heavily on topological error correction codes like the surface code, underscoring the need for efficient and adaptable decoding methods, especially in the presence of faulty measurements. This study transforms the full fault-tolerant decoding problem into a learning process involving a decoder interacting with a code environment, to which reinforcement learning principles can be applied to develop effective decoding tools. Using deepQ learning as an example, we successfully created rapid surface code decoders capable of handling multiple types of noise models. Our results show that these reinforcement learning decoders can outperform existing approaches, such as belief propagation and semi-definite programming, in both simulated and hardware environments, especially when faced with complex noise scenarios. Moreover, we found that these decoders can learn to adapt to changing noise patterns even if the underlying environment does not change. Ultimately, this research enables the creation of surface code decoders that can effectively handle the errors in large-scale quantum computing systems. Experimental evidence suggests that these decoders can also provide benefits when used on simpler, more traditional decoders, potentially offering a versatile tool for addressing error correction in quantum computing. A common issue in machine learning lies in striking a balance between optimizing performance and robustly handling out-of-distribution (OoD) scenarios. Certain methods rely on complex penalty terms that can be difficult to optimize. Our proposed method, a regularization technique, constructs rich features from the in-distribution data to penalize the model for overfitting. By employing a simplified approach, our approach's computational demands are comparable to that of a standard model. Experiments demonstrate that our method achieves a notable improvement over existing solutions, performing on par with innovative optimization methods in well-optimized scenarios, while also exhibiting enhanced OoD handling capabilities. Notably, our approach's benefits extend to both linear regression and deep learning settings. To further empower the model, we offer two optional features: dynamically adjusting the penalty term based on the data's complexity and incorporating the use of few-shot ood examples during training. Furthermore, we provide a theoretical justification for our approach and conduct an in-depth analysis of the model's properties to offer insights into its performance. Ultimately, our proposed method, dubbed RICH, allows for a seamless balance between performance, robustness, and optimization-related requirements. A comprehensive repository containing the code and datasets to reproduce the results is available at https://github.com/alexmnk/rich. Monolithic CMOS sensors featuring small collection electrodes are gaining popularity
due to their high signal quality and resistance to electrical interference.
However, these sensors have a limited active area due to the layout of the
periphery, which can be mitigated by using thin active layers.
This study investigates the properties of p-on-n CMOS sensors manufactured in
different thicknesses and featuring various substrate materials.
Three CMOS sensor prototypes with active sensor thicknesses of 300 micrometers,
400 micrometers, and 500 micrometers were designed, and the corresponding
beam-echo tests were performed to determine their lateral resistivity.
The results indicate that reducing the thickness from 300 micrometers to 500
micrometers leads to a significant enhancement, decreasing the required distance
for the beam to traverse by nearly 40%.
In addition, the study compares the properties of the monolithic CMOS sensors built
on 200mm wafer substrates with a resistivity of 10-20 ohm-cm and 500mm wafer
substrates with a much higher resistivity of above 100 ohm-cm.
The 500mm wafer material yields a substantial improvement, with the lateral
resistivity decreasing by approximately 25% when the thickness is kept constant.
The research data on these prototype sensors will significantly benefit the CLICTD
detector design, which is a monolithic small collection-electrode technology
demonstrator, by allowing for optimized detector design and enhanced detector
performance. The study's findings will also have a range of applications in both
particle physics and medical imaging. The study's data and related information is

Our fast atmospheric self-coherent camera (FASCAM) technique has shown significant promise in recent years by utilizing the properties of speckles under the influence of turbulence to determine the phase structure of a laser beam after it passes through the atmosphere. This approach offers an attractive alternative to traditional wavefront sensing techniques, particularly when resources are limited and a rapid, wide-field-of-view image is essential. Building on this success, we have successfully implemented the FASCAM technique on a testbed at the Santa Cruz Extreme Adaptive Optics Laboratory. By capturing in real-time, our setup comprises an 80 x 80 pixel sensor, a laser with a 632.8nm wavelength, and a 1.25-meter path length for the laser beam to travel through, mimicking the atmosphere's effects. Notably, our system has achieved a remarkable 300 kHz frame rate, which surpassed our expectations. This achievement has enabled us to explore the potential of FASCAM for the first time. This research marks a significant breakthrough and opens doors for high-speed, wide-field-of-view imaging applications across various fields, including astronomy, laser communication, and target tracking. Moreover, our results also demonstrate the capabilities of focal plane wavefront control by modulating the intensity of speckles in real-time, which could have significant implications for the future development of sensing and communication systems. This study develops a novel integration method for simulating multiple collisions between particles over different time intervals. The method combines a contact model to account for elastic and plastic collisions using a unique formula that considers the time elapsed since the particles' separation. Due to its explicit nature, the method doesn't rely on the solution of complex equations, making it highly suitable for simulation at the particle level. The method is further simplified by applying a fixed time step for all particles, thereby significantly reducing the computational overhead and allowing it to be efficiently coupled with existing finite element methods. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through various numerical examples, including scenarios of a particle colliding with a rigid wall and multiple particles interacting with each other. The results from these examples verify that the method can accurately simulate collision events using a time step that may be larger than the typical friction coefficient, thus offering a significant performance enhancement over traditional methods. The study concludes by comparing the new integration method with the contact dynamics method, revealing that the new method is substantially more efficient while still producing comparable results. Several local authorities face challenges in deploying advanced automated road
condition assessment tools due to their limited availability or high implementation
costs. While these platforms offer high precision, they are often country-specific
or industry-bound, making it difficult to adapt them to different settings. To
overcome these obstacles and streamline the process, we suggest a multi-faceted
approach that integrates transfer learning and combines both conventional and
deep-learning techniques. Our proposed method leverages a vast, globally relevant
road damage image dataset to enable the development of a universal roadmap for
road condition assessment. We put this approach to the test by adapting the
model to detect road damages in Czech and Slovak environments, achieving a high
success rate along the way. The results demonstrate that with minimal adjustments,
the model can deliver exceptional results even in unfamiliar settings. Moreover,
by leveraging the advantages of convolutional neural networks, the implementation
cost of our approach can be substantially reduced. Consequently, the proposed
method offers a cost-effective and efficient solution for local authorities to
rapidly and affordably deploy advanced road condition assessment tools. Our
proposed method also provides valuable insights for developers when working with
road damage images, including the essential features to focus on and the tasks to
target. Additionally, we make available the source code and the trained models for
public access, enabling other researchers to build upon our work and adapt the
model to their specific needs. Our ultimate goal is to make advanced road condition
assessment technology more accessible and affordable for all local authorities.

Individuals within the criminal justice system frequently suffer from mental health disorders. To address this, some jurisdictions enforce mental health treatment as part of probation, although the impact is rarely studied. We examine how a court-ordered therapy program, specifically Multidimensional Family Therapy, impacts the mental health and criminal behavior of convicted individuals. Utilizing data on nearly 25,000 defendants in Indiana between 2009 and 2015, our analysis reveals that those undergoing this therapy experience reduced rates of violent and property crimes by 13% and 10%, respectively, and also exhibit improved mental health as indicated by lower scores on the Offender Assessment Tool. Our results suggest that this particular type of therapy is effective in both reducing crime and improving mental health. Interestingly, the benefits are more pronounced among defendants who are younger, have a stronger history of crime, or are male. Additionally, the effects are more noticeable when the program is implemented shortly after conviction. To further investigate the underlying mechanisms, we design a novel test that assesses the relationship between therapy and the probability of incarceration. Our results indicate that the benefits of the program are not simply a result of more frequent police interactions, as we also find a significant decrease in the likelihood of incarceration. More broadly, our research highlights the potential for therapy to reduce crime and improve mental health, ultimately suggesting that such programs could serve as a valuable tool for policymakers. From a practical perspective, our findings imply that increasing the availability and duration of these therapy programs, particularly Multidimensional Family Therapy, could lead to improved outcomes for both mental health and criminal behavior. From a theoretical standpoint, our research demonstrates the effectiveness of a specific type of therapy while also emphasizing the importance of considering the underlying characteristics of the individuals undergoing treatment as well as the specific context in which the treatment is administered. Furthermore, our analysis highlights the value of utilizing observational data and relies on a flexible econometric approach that allows us to control for various factors while also preserving the inherent complexity of the data. Finally, our study also shows the potential applications of this research, such as reducing crime and improving mental health through the implementation of evidence-based therapy, while also highlighting the need for further policy-relevant research. Additionally, our results also underscore the need for a more comprehensive support system that extends beyond incarceration to better address the mental health needs of individuals within the criminal justice system. Radio maps are being explored as a promising approach to equip advanced wireless networks with situational awareness. They will likely serve a crucial function in enabling UAV communications by allowing the assessment of signal strength and interference levels at unknown locations. Different from conventional radio map estimation techniques, which depend on uncontrolled sensor measurements, a new method proposes that a UAV collect data at designated locations along a carefully planned route to quickly obtain a reliable map. This route is optimized using a measure that assesses the gain from new information collected at each stop, taking into account the cost of propellant required to reach that location. Our results show that this approach allows the UAV to obtain a map with the same level of accuracy as alternative methods, which may require the collection of more data, following a pattern that changes in predictable ways as the number of measurement variables and the signal-to-noise ratio increase. Additionally, two algorithms have been developed to implement this approach, one of which uses the Zangwill-Gardner algorithm to optimize the route and another that uses simulated annealing to overcome limitations in the algorithms' ability to handle complex problems efficiently. This alternative method has been shown to perform well when the number of measurement variables is low but may struggle with higher numbers of variables without becoming impractical. Finally, our results have been compared to those of a method that uses deep neural networks to obtain a map, which was found to perform well but may struggle to explain its decisions. This study, which used simulation data based on a widely used outdoor environment, has shown that these approaches, which prioritize efficiency and reliability, can perform well in wireless communications applications. It is our hope that these results will serve as a foundation for future research into the development of reliable maps for use in UAV communications. This research presents a novel approach to identifying unusual patterns in time series data, particularly those influenced by recurring events. The method employs Hidden Markov Models (HMs) to analyze data and assesses anomalies by comparing expected model behaviors with actual outcomes. Our ANOM_HMM model calculates anomalies as discrepancies between these two elements, providing both quantitative and qualitative results that highlight the magnitude and timing of deviations. This information can be leveraged to develop predictive models, reduce false positives, and guide human decision-making. To validate our approach, we analyzed airline delay data and demonstrated its effectiveness in comparing real-world patterns with artificially manipulated data representing system failures. A comprehensive evaluation of the ANOM_HMM model revealed its ability to accurately detect anomalies in complex systems characterized by recurring events. Furthermore, this method provides valuable insights that can contribute to the development of more sophisticated anomaly detection algorithms. To facilitate the use of this method in practical applications, we have made the ANOM_HMM code available on GitHub. By integrating this method into existing automated systems, we can minimize false alarms and enhance decision-making processes, ultimately leading to more efficient operations. At the same time, this analysis provides valuable context that can be used to identify areas for further improvement in system development. To summarize, the ANOM_HMM method offers a versatile solution for identifying unusual patterns in time series data, particularly those influenced by recurring events, and this method has been successfully validated through our analysis of airline delay data. This approach provides accurate results, provides insights into the anomalies, and has been made available to facilitate its use in a variety of applications. By integrating this method into existing automated systems, we can optimize operations, improve decision-making processes, and identify areas for further improvement. Furthermore, this analysis provides a clear framework that can be used to develop more sophisticated anomaly detection algorithms in the future. Our technique involves the automatic manipulation of non-speaker sounds in a dataset to create new speaker paths. We test this method on a Minimax English corpus and compare it to three established techniques. We find that while our approach doesn't quite match the performance of the more labor-intensive methods, it does offer a viable alternative when resources are limited. Additionally, combining it with other techniques leads to superior results. We demonstrate that using this approach to generate a large amount of data can yield better outcomes than using smaller, more intricate datasets. Finally, a combination of our approach and two established techniques leads to outstanding results. We also offer an open-source platform for those looking to replicate our results. The platform includes code for generating the augmented data as well as a full training protocol. We hope this will enable others to build upon our work in the future. Furthermore, we propose an optimization approach to adjust the privacy settings and increase data utility. Our experimental outcomes demonstrate that depending attributes significantly influence privacy breaches and negatively impact data utility, while the optimized privacy settings substantially improve data utility while maintaining reliable privacy protections. Our findings contribute to the development of more efficient one-sided differential privacy systems. Unlike other compatibility models that rely on a fixed set of visual attributes and attribute values, VICTOR benefits from the advantages of contrastive pre-training. On one hand, it incorporates a proprietary fashion dataset to generate visual features for outfit items and attributes, enabling more precise compatibility analysis. On the other hand, it leverages a contrastive loss function to self-supervise the extraction of semantically significant features from item images and attributes. Following the pre-training phase, VICTOR achieves exceptional performance on the Fashionista benchmark, outperforming existing benchmarks and showcasing the effectiveness of contrastive pre-training for visual incompatibility analysis. The model's source code and model weights are available for public access at https://github.com/whaiwhai/VICTOR.

As the number of devices contributing to cross-device federated learning grows, synchronizing updates can significantly reduce efficiency. The FedBuff algorithm mitigates this limitation by enabling asynchronous updates and securely aggregated data sharing, thus allowing for faster convergence of models despite time differences and network disruptions. Building on the FedBuff framework for asynchronous learning, our research introduces new challenges by exploring its performance under models with unbounded gradient values. To address this issue, we develop a novel version of FedBuff, specifically known as FedBuff-U, tailored for asynchronous learning with possibly unbounded gradients. FedBuff-U incorporates a convergence-proven technique to limit gradient amplification and ensures the algorithm still converges to the global optimum. Our experiments demonstrate that FedBuff-U achieves comparable performance to FedBuff in various FL scenarios, while outperforming traditional FL methods by a significant margin. Additionally, FedBuff-U exhibits superior performance over a FedAvg-based method designed for asynchronous learning with unbounded gradients. Our study also includes an in-depth analysis of the theoretical performance of FedBuff-U and observes that in practice, it often surpasses this theoretical benchmark. Our findings indicate that FedBuff-U offers a more robust solution for FL applications, particularly when dealing with delayed updates and potentially infinite gradient values. Our code is publicly available for verification. We examine isothermic surfaces with a Hopf differential that decomposes into a real function and a specific quadratic differential with a singular point. However, this differential is nonzero and holomorphic throughout the rest of the surface except at this singular point. By focusing on a patch excluding the singular point, we find new isothermic surfaces applying the Darboux and Calapso transformations. Furthermore, we investigate how the transformed patches behave as they approach the singular point and check for continuity in that region. Additionally, we look at what happens in the modified patches after the transformation. Interestingly, for certain special cases, the transformed patches will be geodesically convex. Using specific examples, we show how previously known isothermic surface families can be rederived using our approach and that other novel surface families are generated. Lastly, we apply our method to produce geodesic loxodromics for isothermic surfaces, which had not been seen before. With further analysis, the characteristics of geodesic loxodromics in these transformed patches could be explored. Our method can also be applied to other isothermic surface families with different properties. Finally, we suggest a few possible research paths based on our findings.

The focus of this research is on open knowledge base questions, a problem tackled through the OKBQ challenge, where the key to answering these questions lies in understanding the dynamics of knowledge graphs. To capture these temporal relationships, participants must employ models that can handle temporal data or align regular knowledge graphs with temporally aware graphs. Our solution relies on a technique that involves translating temporal properties into regular relationships, thus enabling the use of established models. To further enhance our model's performance, we employed various techniques such as negative sampling, inverse regularization, and knowledge graph embedding's negative phase. Ultimately, our approach earned us a spot among the top quartile of submissions to the OKBQ challenge 2021, without requiring any sophisticated temporal models. The source code for our solution is available on GitHub.

While widely used, such plots have significant drawbacks, particularly when working with large datasets and intricate models. For instance, they fail to account for the interplay between variables, and the predicted output is often smoothed, which can mask outliers. Furthermore, PDPs only provide information about individual data points and do not offer a global perspective on the contribution of each feature to the model's performance. To address these limitations, we propose an alternative debugging method that relies on the Shapley value, a mathematical framework that assigns a value to each feature based on its contribution to the model's performance in various scenarios. Our approach, referred to as Value-Based Data Debugging (VBD2), involves using the Shapley value to identify subsets of features that collectively contribute significantly to the model's performance. By selecting these features, data analysts can isolate influential variables and gain a deeper understanding of the model's behavior. Our proposed debugger, VBD2, can operate at multiple levels, including individual data points, datasets, and even entire data sets grouped by specific conditions. This paper delves into a Steklov-Robin eigenvalue problem for the Laplacian in a particular class of annular domains. Specifically, we examine a setup involving a larger open set $\Omega_0$, a smaller ball of radius $r$, and consider a first eigenvalue in this scenario where both the Steklov and Robin boundary conditions are imposed. We employ a variety of mathematical techniques, including a functional setup and the von Dupont iteration scheme, to derive this expression. We also examine how the Steklov and Robin eigenvalue limits compare when $r$ tends towards zero. Lastly, this paper focuses on the smoothness of the first Steklov eigenfunction when the Steklov constant is nonzero and the Robin constant is zero, and we demonstrate that the first Steklov eigenfunction can be both the first Robin eigenfunction and the first Steklov eigenfunction, depending on specific parameter choices. We address the critical issue of hypergraph hyperedge detection in supervised settings, where the desired outcomes - hyperedges - are not readily available but the individual node characteristics are known. This involves using node attributes to predict target subgraph structures within complex networks, such as identifying closely related genes within a genetic interaction map or understanding the underlying structure of stock market relationships. To tackle this challenge, we present a two-stage supervised hypergraph reconstruction framework that incorporates the constraints of both node and target subgraph features. This framework first generates optimal hyperedges by optimizing the adherence to predicted subgraph patterns in a supervised learning context, then assesses the resulting hypergraph using the normalized mutual information metric for validation. To evaluate the framework's performance, we developed two real-world applications involving disease-related genetic maps and European stock market analysis, which demonstrate the framework's ability to accurately identify hyperedges and outperform alternative methods in supervised hypergraph reconstruction. The implemented approach is also adaptable for a wide range of applications. The source code for this project is available at https://github.com/charleshwang89/SVR_Hypergraph. Further details on the code and dataset can be found at https://charleshwang89.github.io/SVR_Hypergraph.

This research proposes an effective method for defect detection in patterned fabric images. Our approach leverages Gabor features combined with Histogram of Gradients to enhance defect recognition, especially on fabric with intricate patterns. Additionally, we integrate a Haar transform framework into the image processing pipeline to improve the method's efficiency and adaptability. Our findings reveal that this strategy outperforms existing techniques, yielding superior results and reduced computational requirements. To further refine this method, we develop a low-rank decomposition strategy to concentrate on areas with minimal information and accelerate the processing time. Our experiments demonstrate that this modified approach maintains exceptional accuracy while significantly reducing the computation time. Our proposed method has been thoroughly evaluated on a extensive dataset, and the source code is available for reproduction. The study explores the impact of key parameters on the method's performance and recommends optimal settings for successful implementation. Our method has been successfully tested and shown excellent results, with a notable average precision of 97.15% for training and 96.15% for testing. Moreover, we provide a detailed analysis of the influence of low-rank parameters on the method's efficiency. Our research contributes a novel defect detection approach that balances accuracy and efficiency, and the associated code enables the reproduction of our results for the benefit of the research community. Our method can be applied to various patterned fabric images for defect identification, and we anticipate that our work will serve as a valuable reference for similar studies in the future. Lastly, we highlight the potential for our method to detect defects in color fabric images by incorporating color features, which represents an exciting area of further research and development. To enhance the robustness of target-driven visual navigation systems powered by deep reinforcement learning, we introduce an information-theoretic constraint to the learning process. By maximizing the correlation between the agent's navigation actions and the resulting visual transformations, the agent makes more informed decisions, effectively learning a predictive model of the environment. Through a variational generative approach, the agent learns to anticipate the impact of its actions, utilizing this predictive capability to guide its navigation. As a result, the agent exhibits improved performance on complex indoor and outdoor datasets, even in the absence of explicit reward functions. Moreover, the agent demonstrates heightened adaptability and error resilience, facilitating navigation in unseen environments and recovering from navigation disruptions. The developed framework offers a comprehensive DLRL paradigm that surpasses traditional target-driven navigation systems in both performance and robustness. Thorough experimental evaluations and detailed analysis are provided to substantiate the efficacy of our approach. Furthermore, the method exhibits promising applications in multiple fields, including robotics and computer vision, as demonstrated by our navigation trials utilizing a mobile robot and eye-tracking technology. Specifically, the method has been successfully used to navigate a mobile robot around a cluttered indoor environment using a camera, as well as guide a human via eye-tracking to recover from a self-imposed navigation distraction in an outdoor setting. Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research introduces TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of the text-based game environment that achieves a remarkable one million actions per second, a whopping 3333 times faster than prior games.
By leveraging recent breakthroughs in near-memory processing, TextWorldExpress maintains this impressive speed even when processing intricate game states and performing detailed output. 
Our findings demonstrate the potential for significant increases in game performance, with text-based game environments capable of reaching speeds of tens of thousands of actions per second. 
TextWorldExpress is now freely accessible at https://github.com/basilevignon/TWX-Editor/. 
Future research can build upon this platform to push the boundaries of virtual agent testing. 
Our code and data are available at https://github.com/basilevignon/TWX-Editor/.

A key concept in robot learning is manipulability, representing the geometric relationship between end-effector motion and joint rotation. This relationship is essential for training robots to execute natural movements. While robot-specific design factors and wear can significantly affect manipulability, these factors typically go unchecked in learning algorithms. Our approach develops a new method to adapt robot manipulability based on human data, accounting for the unique configurations and geometries of each robot. By creating a continuous connection between human and robot configurations, our method utilizes the intrinsic characteristics of the configuration manifold to synchronize the templates. Additionally, our method leverages parallel transport to ensure smooth adaptation and applies a modified Iterative Closest Point algorithm to handle complex geometric distortions. We test our method on two tasks: grasping in a simulated 3D environment and manipulating a real robotic arm. Our results show that with only a few human demonstrations, our algorithm enables robots to perform tasks based on human expertise, even with significant design or wear-related differences. Moreover, our method allows robots to transition seamlessly between human and adapted configurations, a feature we term "geometric generalization." Our approach represents a significant advancement in robot learning, particularly for tasks involving complex geometric complexities, and paves the way for the development of more adaptable and collaborative robots. Policy iteration comes with computational drawbacks in large-scale Markov decision processes due to a local quadratic contraction rate and the costliness of its iterations for many states. Informed by its relation to the semismooth Newton method and the efficiency of its inexact variations, inexact policy iteration, a class of algorithms for large-scale finite MDPs with $\mathcal{O}(K^2)$ local contraction rate, was introduced. This rate makes inexact policy iteration appealing, but its implementation proves challenging due to the need for precise computation in each iteration. We address this limitation with inexact GMRES policy iteration, a specific algorithm that exploits the efficiency of GMRES to lower the computational burden of inexact policy iteration while maintaining its favorable contraction properties. We analyze inexact GMRES policy iteration and demonstrate that it retains the $\mathcal{O}(K^2)$ local contraction rate, thereby outperforming standard policy iteration. Moreover, our analysis involves the creation of a novel technique for estimating the policy iteration sequence, known as the epsilon-truncation error measure, to assess the algorithm's performance and establish its convergence. We validate the efficacy of inexact GMRES policy iteration through numerical experiments, showing that it surpasses both standard policy iteration and the inexact policy iteration algorithm with a linear solver in various scenarios. Specifically, our results reveal that inexact GMRES policy iteration often converges within a fraction of the iterations required by these alternative methods. Thus, inexact GMRES policy iteration emerges as a reliable and efficient tool for solving large-scale MDPs. We make the implementation of inexact GMRES policy iteration publicly available through a Python package called ipiPy. This package includes a range of algorithmic variations that cater to distinct problem specifications, such as when the transition matrix is known or unknown, and whether the reward function is non-affine or affine. We also provide a module for solving reward-based policy iteration, a feature that distinguishes our ipiPy package from other existing solvers. We anticipate that inexact GMRES policy iteration will serve as a vital solution to a broader family of semismooth and nonsmooth optimization problems, encompassing finite MDPs, vector MDPs, and POMDPs, and that the ipiPy package will continue to evolve to meet the evolving needs of the optimization community. Finally, we outline several avenues for future research that these results have enabled. This paper examines the solution to an inverse problem presented by expensive computer simulations of complex real-life scenarios. Specifically, researchers focused on an expensive hydrological model designed to generate realistic data for Athens, Georgia, USA. To efficiently handle the large datasets produced by such simulators, an approach involves first selecting key points to approximate the output, and then applying a specialized method to estimate optimal input parameters at those points, while accounting for any uncertainty in the solution. A comprehensive simulation-based study compares the proposed method with alternative techniques and demonstrates their relative performance. Furthermore, the study highlights the computational benefits of this approach by illustrating how to seamlessly integrate it with existing methods that approximate outputs at random points, resulting in a computationally efficient scheme. Finally, the paper includes an example showing how to utilize this efficient scheme to create ensemble members and perform probabilistic simulations, ultimately facilitating the quantification of uncertainty in the simulated outcomes. The implemented methods are made available through a dedicated R package called ParParTS. Experimental data and related code can be accessed at https://github.com/parparts/ParParTS. Additionally, the R code used in the study can be found at https://github.com/parparts/ParParTS_code. A separate document on this repository provides the necessary setup to replicate all the results presented in the paper. The proposed method has numerous potential applications across various fields, including engineering, environmental science, and epidemiology, among others. Examples of suitable problems and relevant outlets have been outlined in a supplementary resource. Key words: expensive computer simulators, parameter estimation, multiple contour estimation, active subspace, kernel ridge regression, Gaussian processes, Monte Carlo sampling, probabilistic simulations. Research into learning from label distributions has shown that leveraging neighborhood information can enhance learning, particularly when dealing with outlier labels. Nevertheless, the theoretical underpinnings of utilising local queries in the context of robust learning remain relatively unexplored. This study delves into the robust learning paradigm where the teacher's labels may be affected by noisy factors in addition to being outlier-labeled. We develop model-agnostic bounds that illustrate how utilizing local queries can improve learning outcomes by quantifying the benefits of querying nearby data points. Our analysis demonstrates that incorporating local queries can substantially reduce dependence on the hypothesis' norm, replacing it with the norm of the query matrix and the maximum degree of the graph on which the data is distributed, thus offering a more favourable risk bound. We also introduce a new regularisation technique that exploits the structure of graph-based local queries, and demonstrate the efficacy of our approach through empirical evaluations on synthetic and real-world datasets. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/DeepMind/local_queries_robust_learning.

For the first time, fragmentation functions for jets associated with a lone photon have been measured in collisions involving protons and a lead-lead nucleus. This analysis used data from the CMS experiment at the CERN LHC, operating at a proton-proton center-of-mass energy of 5.02 TeV. The fragmentation functions for jets above 30 GeV were determined in events with a high-transverse-momentum photon, above 60 GeV, where charged particles with a minimum transverse momentum of 1 GeV were tracked within a narrow cone around the jet axis. In collisions with 0-80 percent centrality, jets in the most forward direction displayed the same fragmentation as those in proton-proton collisions, while those in the most central collisions showed an increase in the number of charged particles within the jet by 12 percent relative to proton-proton collisions, at a transverse momentum of 4 GeV. This observation indicates that photons can effectively serve as quark regulators, and that the fragmentation modifications are confined primarily to the quark partons. Additionally, the data agree with Monte Carlo simulations that incorporate medium effects, but differ from those without such effects. This analysis represents the first direct evidence of parton modification as partons traverse the quark-gluon plasma. Furthermore, this observation is consistent with the idea that photons can be used as calibration tools to study the interactions between charged particles and the jet medium. Finally, this analysis highlights the potential for future photon-jet measurements to serve as a reliable test of theoretical models in the study of jet modification and its application to the study of quark and gluon jets. At a minimum, this analysis underscores the importance of continuing to collect large datasets to ensure that the jet modification phenomenon is thoroughly understood. To that end, this analysis has provided new insights and has set a new standard for future research into the jet modification phenomenon. This method enhances numerical precision with a reduced number of grid points for PDF evolution, making it a valuable tool for further PDSD research. The proposed method is detailed in a user-friendly code called \textit{ChebPDFT}. The code's versatility enables easy integration into various particle physics frameworks and enables the exploration of previously inaccessible regions of the phase space for PDSDs, thus facilitating more accurate double-parton scattering calculations. The advent of this method also enables the simultaneous investigation of PDFs and PDSDs utilizing the same resources, thus significantly decreasing computation time and costs. The proposed method is validated through visual inspections and quantitative analyses that demonstrate its precision and efficiency. The findings are then compared with another existing method, demonstrating the superiority of the presented approach. Finally, we showcase the method's capacity by examining the ratio of inclusive $p$-$p$ to $e^+-e^-$ high-mass dijet cross-sections, which could serve as a $BPDS$ sensitivity probe, highlighting its potential in distinguishing double-parton interactions from other non-collinear processes. The dynamics of a liquid film on a fiber heavily depend on the boundary conditions at the liquid-solid interface. When the liquid adheres to the fiber, a film forms that is subject to the Plateau-Rayleigh instability, leading to liquid droplet detachment. However, if the liquid slips along the fiber, a new instability mechanism emerges, which can cause more rapid droplet breakup. A recent asymptotic analysis of this problem has been revised to include a general fiber shape and the effects of liquid property variations. A new model has been developed to predict droplet ejection and to determine the critical conditions for breakup, which are influenced by the slip length, liquid property differences, and liquid-air surface tension. A particular case where the liquid and fiber have the same density shows that the slip enhancement effect can increase the breakup length by up to 70% over the adherent scenario. Moreover, the model has been validated using numerical simulations, which also reveal additional modes of instability. A theoretical description has been developed for these modes, as well as a new type of droplet deformation, and both have been compared with the numerical results. A design for microdroplet generators has also been proposed based on these findings. Experimental verification of these theoretical predictions is anticipated. Moreover, the range of parameters where the slip-enhanced breakup effect prevails has been determined and found to be quite extensive, covering two orders of magnitude, and is largely independent of the liquid and fiber materials used. The Fisher-KPP equation, a reaction-diffusion equation, was first introduced by Fisher in 1935 to model allele spread within genetic populations, and later by Kolmogorov in 1937 in a broader context. Its analytical solution has been extensively sought after due to its widespread applications in modeling population growth and spread. Fortunately, a full analytical solution was found as early as 1952 by Feller, consisting of a singular curve and a curved boundary separated by a critical value. Since then, the singular curve solution was further analyzed by Ward and Pelletier in 2007. Our work presents an alternative and more fundamental approach to deriving the singular curve solution, yielding a general formula applicable to any dimension of the diffusion process. Moreover, our method reveals the underlying symmetry of the singular curve solution, allowing us to apply it to model various population growth and spread scenarios in one, two, and three dimensions. To illustrate the versatility of our solution, we apply it to model the spread of COVID-19 in the United States. Finally, our method is also adaptable for modeling non-uniform initial conditions. The resulting solutions respect conservation laws and are accurate down to the level of individual cities, as demonstrated by our example using Atlanta, Georgia. Our novel solution provides a versatile tool for modeling various population growth and spread scenarios, offering a precise match with real-world data down to the level of small areas. As a result, our model can be used for accurate and precise predictions of the spread of infectious diseases and other population dynamics phenomena. Species distribution analysis is a crucial aspect of ecological research, and occupancy modeling has become a preferred approach due to its ability to account for false positives. However, occupancy models that consider only a single species or pair of species may not be sufficient for understanding multi-species community dynamics. The development of unified software to fit single, multi, and integrated species occupancy models will enable researchers to explore these alternatives and make more informed decisions. The spOccupancy package offers a comprehensive solution, providing a composable framework for modeling various species interactions and incorporating auxiliary data to improve model performance. This article serves as a guide to the spOccupancy package, outlining its key features and providing practical implementation examples. Additionally, we highlight the package's capabilities through a community ecology case study involving bird species co-occurring in Colorado's montane forests. The spOccupancy package is publicly accessible on CRAN, along with accompanying documentation and tutorial vignettes. It includes models for single, multi, and integrated species occupancy models, as well as auxiliary data, time series, and multi-species combinations. The package's flexibility allows users to create their own custom model combinations by incorporating newly developed specifications. The model's flexibility was demonstrated in the community ecology case study, which involved analyzing data from bird observations collected in Colorado's montane forests. The analysis utilized multi-species occupancy models that integrated auxiliary data, time series, and species co-occurring in the region. The results from this case study provided evidence of significant species interactions, highlighting the spOccupancy package's ability to improve model fit and accuracy when accounting for complex community dynamics. To study the movement of heavy particles into a rising turbulent plume, we conducted experiments using a plume that rises through a body of water containing particles of varying densities and sizes. The particles were placed at the base of a container and a hole was pierced at the top, allowing a controlled water jet to rise and interact with the particles as the container is rotated. Due to density differences between the particles and the fluid, they do not have the same upward velocity as the plume, which causes them to lag behind and become trapped in a vortex formed at the base of the container. As a result, the particles are caught in a secondary circulation caused by the rotation of the container. Because of particle size and density differences, their behavior is affected in distinct ways. Larger particles tend to move less than the fluid and remain near the base of the container, while those with lower densities are able to travel further and even leave the container when its rotation is stopped. The particles' movement is also influenced by their size relative to the turbulence created by the plume and by the forces acting on them due to their difference in density, which can cause them to move in a zigzag pattern. Our research found that these particles are able to rise by exploiting the momentum transferred to them by the plume's turbulence and by the forces acting on them due to their difference in density, which can cause them to accelerate upwards. Based on our findings, we were able to develop a theoretical model that accurately predicts the particles' movement and provides results consistent with our experiments. The range of parameters in our experiments, where the particles' movement was influenced by their size, shape, and density, as well as the plume's velocity and turbulence, spans several decades and includes various natural and engineering systems, such as ocean currents, where plankton move through the water and are caught in whirlpools, and coffee froth, where particles are carried upwards by the plume created by hot water. McMini is a well-established, efficient model checker for multithreaded C programs, relying on a dynamic prediction-based reduction in state technique. This approach, although effective, presents a limitation in that it confines the developer to using a fixed prediction algorithm. This paper introduces McMini2, an upgradable version of the original model checker, incorporating a flexible, programmable reduction in state mechanism. This innovation empowers developers to create their own prediction strategies, thereby expanding the range of programs that can be safely checked. Moreover, McMini2 retains all the key characteristics of the original model checker that contribute to its performance, such as low memory usage and fast path execution. As a result, McMini2 is capable of efficiently modeling thousands of real C multithreaded functions. Furthermore, McMini2's design facilitates the comparison of various prediction algorithms' effectiveness, with experimental findings indicating that McMini2 can detect half to two-thirds more errors than McMini when utilizing a previously established algorithm. Additionally, McMini2's modular architecture enables the integration of multiple prediction methods, thereby enhancing its overall performance and detecting a total of 1,016 additional errors when compared to McMini. These outcomes validate the modified design and validate the potential for further innovation based on McMini. Crucially, McMini2 is backwards compatible and can run all the original McMini tests, as well as detect additional errors. Finally, McMini2's open design and the availability of toolkits allow other researchers to experiment with novel prediction strategies, solidifying McMini2's status as a public model checker and promoting collaborative research in this domain. Details about McMini2, along with its implementation and 41 distinct prediction strategies, are available online at http://mcmini2.ms.unimontpellier.fr/. Additionally, McMini2 has been integrated into the Veridis verification platform, where it can be accessed via a web interface at http://veridis.ms.unimontpellier.fr/. This integration has facilitated the joint analysis of tens of thousands of real multithreaded C functions, yielding valuable insights and best practices for model checking. Specifically, our research uncovered four key factors that contribute to state space explosion, while also identifying the fast path as a pivotal component in efficient model checking. The global WhatsApp user base relies heavily on the app's personal, group, and voice/video call features for communication. As one of the most popular messaging apps, it plays a significant role in information dissemination, particularly in personal conversations and smaller groups. The spread of misinformation through social media platforms like WhatsApp has become a significant concern, prompting WhatsApp's parent company, Facebook, to introduce a limit on the number of times a message can be forwarded to other users within a single conversation. This study aims to understand the impact of this change, analyzing user behavior, the spread of messages, and the success of anti-misinformation efforts before and after the limitation was implemented. Our research reveals that while the cap may have reduced the scale of misinformation spread within a single conversation, it has not substantially curtailed the app's overall misinformation problem, as it allows larger-scale distributions via an infinite number of conversations. Furthermore, the exact effects of the limitation vary greatly, depending on the type of information and the users involved. Based on our research findings, we suggest three possible next steps: utilizing AI-powered automated message detection, targeting specific, high-risk information types, and collaborating with healthcare professionals and trusted entities to provide users with accurate information. Additionally, we provide an open-source dataset of WhatsApp conversations and propose a framework for evaluating misinformation countermeasures that align with real-world communication practices. This framework is centered on three key metrics: the prevalence of misinformation, information dissemination patterns, and the consistency of user information collections. Our approach can serve as a baseline for evaluating system-level interventions, such as the WhatsApp limitation, as well as other anti-misinformation strategies. Ultimately, our research suggests that a multi-faceted approach that combines technical innovations and collaborative non-technical interventions is necessary to effectively address the complex problem of online misinformation. As a demonstration of our research, we have made available a WhatsApp conversation dataset that can be used for replication purposes, as well as for the development of novel misinformation countermeasures. This dataset can be accessed via the link: https://tinyurl.com/whatsapp-conversations. Additional information about our research can be found at the website: https://misinfo.ai/. Identifying the application protocol is a critical process in network security monitoring that demands a quick and accurate assessment to support detailed traffic analysis. Although pinpointing the application protocol can be challenging, the consequences of misidentification are generally considered minor and manageable. Consequently, most monitoring systems rely on simple and expedient methods to identify application protocols, such as checking for distinctive traffic patterns or examining specific data fields. In this study, three open-source network monitoring tools were evaluated to investigate how they detect dynamic application protocols. Our research revealed that two of these tools are vulnerable to evasion attacks, with the third tool also susceptible to evasion although to a limited extent. Furthermore, our investigation into the detection mechanisms employed by commercial security monitoring systems revealed that the majority rely on simple and easily manipulated methods, such as checking for known traffic patterns or system headers and footers. In contrast, only one out of seven commercial systems and two out of three open-source tools used more sophisticated detection based on anomaly analysis. Based on our research findings, we are sharing two open-source evasion tools, along with documentation and guidelines, to aid researchers in assessing the detection capabilities of network monitoring systems. Additionally, we are publishing a report outlining our research methodology, results, and recommendations for improving detection mechanisms. Our research also raises broader security and privacy concerns, which we discussed in detail, along with potential resolutions. This research presents novel techniques for federated learning that streamline the process of adding new categories to audio classification models. The paper showcases the effectiveness of these techniques in a real-world context, where the existing class labels are inaccessible. Our contributions include a probabilistic Syntactic Pattern Recognition-based method for deriving class transitions from federated model updates, and a dynamic clustering approach to group similar transitions together. This study analyzes data from an online monitoring system of U.S. local news to explore connections between COVID coverage, regional case and death rates, and characteristics of news outlets and their audiences. Using a distinct approach that accounts for varying audience sizes, our results reveal three key findings. Firstly, the amount of local news coverage about COVID exceeds national coverage, with more prominent coverage in areas with higher case and death rates. Secondly, news outlets that have established reputations for in-depth COVID coverage are more likely to report stories about COVID as the pandemic's case and death rates rise in their regions. Lastly, demographic groups that are more likely to receive local news coverage about COVID include older adults and those living in areas with higher case and death rates. These groups also engage more with news through traditional means rather than social media. Our research offers new insights for understanding local news dynamics and highlights the significance of considering audience perspectives and news ecosystem characteristics when analyzing COVID-related news coverage. Ultimately, our findings may facilitate the development of more targeted strategies to disseminate information effectively and enhance public understanding of the pandemic. With the new architectural design, our networks exhibited a pattern similar to that of human children, where easier tasks were initially tackled using one counting method, but a more efficient strategy was employed as the level of difficulty increased. Conversely, the networks with limited internal memory capacity were unable to transition to this more effective method of solving counting problems, instead opting for a single strategy from the outset. Based on these findings, our study provides new insights for developers of cognitive architectures and artificial intelligence systems, informing the design of computational models that can effectively tackle complex problems, particularly those requiring the application of abstract concepts. Specifically, servers utilize DBSCAN with S2PC to cluster the legitimate data majority without acquiring private user data. Concurrently, clients create duplicate models and engage in distance-controlling tests to tailor their submissions towards the predicted normal data center. Our framework is both highly performance-efficient and compatible with existing FL implementations, as demonstrated by our execution of it on mobile devices and MRI image classification. Notably, our results show an impressive enhancement in robustness and a substantial reduction in communication overhead, with MRI image classification exhibiting particular success. Our findings indicate that server-processing and client-uploaded models converge during the same iteration, resulting in a noticeable decrease in training duration. Furthermore, the duplicate model approach and distance control mechanism enable clients to submit models that are both closer to the genuine model and less susceptible to malicious influence, all without exposing their private data. The heart of our motion planning module is a Phases Phases world model, which enables seamless decision-making in diverse environments by breaking down tasks into three distinct phases. This innovation facilitates smooth and precise movement, mimicking the performance of human drivers. The identification of sub-Neptune exoplanets receiving adequate heat from their stars to maintain global temperatures poses a significant challenge in the search for potentially habitable worlds. Oceans on these planets are often hidden from detection due to the surrounding thick atmosphere, which must be dissipated to reveal them. Future missions such as the James Webb Space Telescope will be capable of observing the starlight that passes through the atmosphere and identifies the boundaries between the atmosphere and the solid surface, thereby determining the depth of the starlight absorption. This study examines whether the atmosphere's composition can be inferred from such observations by analyzing the effects of two processes on the atmospheric structure. One process involves the equilibrium between dissolved gases and water, while the other involves gas thermochemistry. We have developed two models that represent these processes and applied them to a representative temperate exoplanet, which we then simulated using two different atmospheres composed mainly of hydrogen and carbon dioxide. Our results show that the two models yield distinct predictions for the atmospheric pressure where the starlight transitions from being fully to partially absorbed. This pressure can serve as a proxy for the pressure at which the starlight passes through the ocean layer, which is essential for characterizing temperate sub-Neptune exoplanets. By comparing the predicted pressures to those obtained from radiative-thermal models, which do not account for atmospheric interactions with the solid surface, we found notable differences, which are driven by the atmosphere's composition and temperature. Importantly, the pressure at the ocean boundary can differ by about 2 orders of magnitude, which corresponds to a difference of up to 1000 km in the radius at which the starlight transitions from being fully to partially absorbed. Our findings highlight the significance of distinguishing between the two processes involved in atmospheric interactions with the solid surface and the gas phase, which is crucial for characterizing the internal structure of temperate sub-Neptune exoplanets. By distinguishing between the two processes, future observations with the James Webb Space Telescope and similar missions can help to constrain the internal structure and composition of these exoplanets, which in turn will facilitate the identification of potentially habitable worlds. Inspired by the classic discrete-time model of nervous activity proposed by McCulloch and Pitts in 1943, a new continuous-time model, known as the McCulloch-Pitts network (MPN), has been developed for sequence learning in spiking neural networks. This model employs local Hebbian synaptic plasticity rules that can efficiently optimize neural weights. Furthermore, the model incorporates a novel synapse type, the 2J1K synapse, to refine its performance. In our research, we have examined the learning capabilities of MPN while minimizing reliance on complex mathematical algorithms. Instead, the model leverages biologically plausible spike-time-dependent synaptic plasticity to adapt the network. Our results demonstrate that MPN can learn complex sequence data, achieve high accuracy, and also exhibit robustness to data noise. To evaluate the model's effectiveness, we have employed well-established datasets, such as the 20 Newsgroups dataset for text categorization and the MNIST dataset for image recognition, and our findings indicate substantial improvements over traditional MPN performance. Our study provides a strong foundation for further development of neural networks inspired by brain function. The associated code is available on the GitHub repository at https://github.com/NeuroPHYSPY/MPN. Our model's open-source implementation is based on the PyTorch deep learning framework. Experimental data, including MPN models, can be accessed via the Phydat repository at https://doi.org/10.6087/C19G1M. Our research is compliant with the IEEE guidelines for reproducibility.

This report outlines the findings of the 2022 European Spallation Source (ESS) ESRF
Challenge, a data compression competition aimed at reducing large-scale synchrotron
radiation data. The challenge posed an unconventional compression problem,
involving unfamiliar image formats, unknown subjects, and unrecognizable features.

out-of-vocabulary image segments and unknown subjects. The report details the
compressor candidates, their performance, and the proposed solutions for improving
compression rates of the top-performing methods, particularly for large datasets. Two
combinatorial approaches were developed to enhance the overall results. The first
approach integrated the top compressors from separate training sets, while the second
utilized a combination of the compressed and original data to explore new possibilities.
The report also includes supplementary information and outlines potential future work
for refining these techniques and applying them to other complex data compression issues. 
Finally, the source code for our implementation is freely available on GitHub at the
specified link.

Given a profinite group G and a G-action on a simplicial space X, we define the homotopy orbit spectrum as the suspension spectrum derived from the homotopy orbit map G \times X → Xⁿ, where Xⁿ represents the homotopy groupoid of X with its n-th iterated suspension. This concept aligns with the classical homotopy orbit functor when G acts trivially. Furthermore, we establish that the homotopy orbit spectrum satisfies the functorial properties of the raw homotopy orbit functor and the smooth Orlik-Pope-Wilson functor. Additionally, we investigate the relationship between the homotopy orbit spectrum and the Orlik-Pope-Wilson functor, particularly in the case of a nilpotent profinite group. Finally, we provide examples and applications, including connections to group cohomology and the study of spaces with G-action. This work has implications for understanding the descriptive complexity of spaces with G-action through the concept of strict homotopy thickness. Specifically, we demonstrate that the homotopy orbit spectrum can be used to express the Whitehead torsion, thereby generalizing the theory of group cohomology with coefficients. This approach also offers a new perspective on the relationship between the homotopy orbit spectrum and the Orlik-Pope-Wilson functor. Moreover, we derive results concerning the homotopy orbit spectrum for certain abelian profinite groups, particularly in the context of Q-adic homotopy theory. Finally, we conclude by outlining future research directions and potential applications. This work should be of interest to researchers in algebraic topology, particularly those working with profinite groups and Q-adic homotopy theory. Additionally, the results presented here may be of use to researchers in group theory and number theory. A major challenge in creating AI models that can automatically process and analyze visually complex documents such as invoices is acquiring a large, high-quality dataset to train these models. Our proposed approach, known as Selective Labeling, streamlines the labeling process by limiting the labels to simple "accept/reject" confirmations for model predictions, rather than extensively marking data as expected outcomes. This technique is supported by an advanced model that can accurately identify potential issues during inference, allowing human labelers to focus on confirming or correct only incorrect predictions. Our results demonstrate that with two human labelers, we can achieve the same level of accuracy as traditional full-labeling methods, while significantly reducing labeling costs by up to 97%. Our model and approach have been validated through real-world applications of two commonly used document analysis tasks: extracting order details from invoices and extracting text from receipts. Additionally, our findings and trained models have been shared on the Datashare platform for further exploration. Moreover, our model can be adapted to various other tasks, as it relies on general algorithmic principles rather than task-specific knowledge. The EuS/InAs interface has gained attention due to its potential to introduce magnetic properties in semiconductor materials, which are essential for various quantum technology applications. Using a computational model that incorporates machine-learned data and density functional theory, we have studied how different bonding configurations at the interface affect the electronic properties. Our findings reveal that the interface energy is minimal when InAs and EuS share electrons, indicating an optimal charge balance. Moreover, our data show that the electronic density at the interface varies significantly based on bonding configurations, with the highest density occurring with InAs donating electrons to EuS. Notably, our simulations suggest that the magnetic moment of Eu is influenced by the bonding configuration, with the highest moment occurring when InAs donates electrons to EuS. Finally, our study of the valence and conduction bands at the interface reveals a 0.4 eV band bend and the presence of unoccupied states near the interface, which could introduce interface states and influence the magnetic properties of the material. Overall, our results provide valuable insights for designing magnetic semiconductor materials using the EuS/InAs interface. This leads to a demonstration of Borel Wadge determinacy within the $\text{ATR}_0+\Pi^1_1$-I system of second-order arithmetic. Deep pruning has become a crucial technique for enhancing the inference efficiency of deployed deep learning models by minimizing their size and computational complexity. However, the conventional end-to-end training approaches for deeply pruned models are hampered by the difficulty in regaining the essential structure of the original neural network. This challenge is compounded by the random nature of many existing pruning methods, which leads to inconsistent results and the need for repeated training. In response to these limitations, we introduce ClickTrain, a novel end-to-end training framework that builds on a previously proposed early pruning method called ePrune. ClickTrain efficiently refines the results of ePrune through a series of accurate fine-grained pruning procedures, including a new analysis-based approach called APrune. By integrating ePrune and APrune, ClickTrain can perform a multi-stage pruning process that maximizes the computational savings while preserving the original neural network's architecture. We demonstrate the effectiveness of ClickTrain by conducting comprehensive experiments on various state-of-the-art models, including ResNet, MobileNet, DenseNet, and TransNet, which showcase the ability of ClickTrain to achieve both substantial pruning rates and superior validation accuracy. Notably, ClickTrain-enabled models can be 3.32 times smaller than their unpruned counterparts while maintaining nearly identical accuracy, or in some cases, even improving accuracy with no reduction in model size. In addition to the evaluation on general top-1 accuracy, we also conducted pairwise performance-cost analysis on various models and found that ClickTrain consistently offers a performance advantage for a given computational cost, or equivalently, a given performance level, ClickTrain can achieve a significantly lower computational cost. In particular, ClickTrain-enabled models can be 2.05 times more efficient than their unpruned counterparts while maintaining nearly identical accuracy, or in some cases, even improving accuracy with no increase in computational cost. The joint analysis of gravitational waves and electromagnetic radiation offers a groundbreaking opportunity to study cosmic events in depth. As more gravitational wave detectors come online, analyzing these ripples will become increasingly important. Although current detectors have limited detection capabilities, advancements in signal processing through deep learning can significantly enhance this, especially for specific types of gravitational wave sources produced by neutron star-black hole mergers. Our research focuses on utilizing deep learning to improve the detection and classification of these merging events by extracting specific features from gravitational waves. Our results indicate that deep learning can accurately classify 94% of mergers and distinguish between various neutron star-black hole merger types with high precision, exceeding current methods' capabilities. We introduce an algorithmic approach to solving constrained Markov decision processes. Our method can solve both the convergence and the finite-horizon problems, providing a straightforward way to calculate the value functions. Our approach is based on iterative policy improvement, with the utility function transformed into a suitable form using the Lagrange primal-dual algorithm. In the case of a convergence problem, the most relevant function is determined by considering the gradient of the value function, which can be challenging to compute directly. To overcome this, we employ the Lagrange multiplier and transform the expression using this variable. Ultimately, our approach yields an iterative algorithm that converges to the optimal policy under specified conditions. Notably, our method does not require knowledge of the gradient of the value function. Our approach was tested on a constrained rock-paper-scissors game and a constrained taxicab problem. In the rock-paper-scissors game, our approach converged to the optimal policy, while in the taxicab problem it yielded a solution that was close to the existing optimal solution. This paper outlines a navigation system consisting of two to five layers, with each layer responsible for a distinct navigation technique. The primary objective of this multi-layered system is to efficiently and effectively navigate through environments where optical technology is impractical. We have implemented a controller that fuses real-time data from both sonar and infrared sensors to enable movement in a specified direction within a designated area, particularly in environments with little to no visibility. We have demonstrated the feasibility of this controller through a video recording of a robotic platform, such as the TurtleBot, navigating around obstacles in a room using the proposed controller. Additionally, our research involves comparing the performance of a single-layered controller that utilizes only sensor fusion to navigate, as well as a multi-layered controller that combines sensor fusion with velocity-based navigation, with the latter showing improved performance in obstacle avoidance situations. However, when the linearity of the environment is taken into account, the single-layered controller exhibits greater efficiency in terms of distance traveled. As a result, the decision-making process can be optimized by selecting the most suitable navigation method based on the characteristics of the environment and the level of obstacle complexity, thereby allowing the system to operate in a more streamlined and effective manner. Experimental findings validate the proposed multi-layered navigation controller and pave the way for its use in a range of robotic applications where diverse environments and obstacle levels are encountered. Crucially, the research presents a novel approach in which machine learning methods are used to determine the optimal navigation strategy for the controller, thereby enabling the navigation controller to be easily adapted to various robotic platforms with minimal modification. Key Words: Multi-Layer Navigation Controller, Sensor Fusion, TurtleBot, Robot Navigation.

A new pessimism-based approach for Bayesian learning in the offline setting is proposed for creating the optimal dynamic treatment regimes. Traditional offline data solutions often result in suboptimal outcomes when the learned policy significantly differs from the true optimal policy. To address this issue, our approach is inspired by Thompson sampling and incorporates a cautious factor, reducing exploration and encouraging the adoption of more established policies when uncertainty is present. By formulating the offline problem as a hidden Markov model, we derive a closed-form expression for the optimal policy. Furthermore, a simple sampling method is developed to simulate the Thompson sampler, and the approach is evaluated using empirical studies in the fields of online advertising and health research, demonstrating improved outcomes with the proposed pessimism-based solution. Our results show that the novel approach outperforms existing solutions, particularly when switching between different policies is costly. Presence-absence data, which record the presence or absence of species at specific locations, present analytical challenges due to their high dimensions and sparse nature.  In this research, we evaluate the performance of seven clustering methods in processing such data under two scenarios: (1) when location coordinates are known, and (2) when they are unknown. Our analysis considers various indices such as the matrix condition number, matrix sparsity, and the use of dimensionality reduction techniques like Multidimensional Scaling.  Our results indicate that methods leveraging location coordinates or using dimensionality reduction perform better than others in both scenarios.  Additionally, our findings suggest that presence-absence data can be effectively clustered using just two axes, and that the application of these clustering methods should be informed by both theoretical and practical considerations. To illustrate the efficacy of our approach, we apply it to two real-world datasets, one related to bird species and another to moth species, and demonstrate that our methods enable the accurate grouping of both birds and moths based on their presence-absence profiles.
