In recent times, salient object detection using RGB and depth information in images has gained significant interest. However, current methods typically focus on these two aspects in separate ways, with RGB-based methods ignoring depth and depth-based methods ignoring RGB information. To address this, we present a unified two-stream structure that leverages both RGB and depth input for more accurate salient object detection. Our proposed method employs a feature extraction module to derive distinct feature sets from the RGB and depth inputs, which are then combined and enhanced by an attention-based fusion module followed by a prediction module. By capturing and combining both color and depth information, we demonstrate improved performance through extensive experimentation. Notably, our method achieves superior results and increased efficiency compared to existing state-of-the-art methods. Computed Tomography (CT) is a significant diagnostic technique used in various medical and industrial applications. Since the x-ray sources used in CT scans emit x-rays of different energies, a reconstructed image from a single energy scan appears faded and distorted, especially when the attenuation coefficients are high. To improve image quality, some CT systems utilize additional sensors or detectors to collect data at multiple energy levels, enabling the reconstruction of not only detailed images but also the separate attenuation coefficients for each material and energy level. Our research focuses on developing a variational regularisation model that can utilise dual-energy data to reconstruct images and their composition while accounting for the non-convex and polyenergetic nature of the CT forward problem. Furthermore, our proposed model can also denoise the reconstructed images. By incorporating a convex penalty term and using a semismooth augmented Lagrange Method (SALM) to solve the optimisation problem, we have successfully applied the model to actual scanner data and compared its performance with traditional techniques and Rintala's model. Our results demonstrate that the reconstructed images and material compositions produced by our proposed model are comparable to those achieved with research-grade dual-source CT scanners. Additionally, our study also examines how the non-convexity of the CT system affects image quality and suggests a way to regularise the solution using Tikhonov regularization. Our work has culminated in a 3D reconstruction software tool that has been utilised to study the composition of various objects such as a chest phantom and a chest phantom with weights. Our approach provides a flexible framework that can be adapted to various CT systems and can serve as a useful diagnostic and research resource. Handwritten Text Recognition (HTR) with limited resources is a complex challenge, primarily due to the absence of a complete alphabet and extensive training datasets. Traditional approaches to address these issues often rely on character-level language models or character segmentation to fill in missing information, whereas existing research has focused on word-level models. Our research proposes a novel method to improve HTR performance in resource-constrained settings by leveraging a language model at the text level. The suggested approach involves creating synthetic training samples on the fly, based on the text transcription provided by the language model, to fine-tune the model in a single iteration. The proposed technique can be applied to both handwritten and typewritten documents. Experimental results on the historical document collection "LibriOcrhi" demonstrate a significant performance boost, with our method achieving a Character Error Rate (CER) of 17.5%, in comparison to a CER of 21.3% when no language model is employed and a CER of 34.6% when no handwritten text correction is applied. Moreover, by integrating the proposed method with existing techniques such as handwriting normalization and neural handwriting modeling, we can attain even better results, with a CER of 13.9 on the same dataset. The source code for our method is publicly available at https://github.com/charlottelm/TextBasedLanguageModel. The "LibriOcrhi" dataset can be accessed via https://github.com/charlottelm/LibriOcrhi. The proposed approach offers a versatile solution to improve HTR performance in diverse settings and can be adapted for various other handwritten document recognition tasks. Additionally, the associated dataset "LibriOcrhi" containing over 300K handwritten pages can be utilized for training and evaluation of deep handwritten text models, with an optional label for text transcription that can enhance the performance of existing models. The "LibriOcrhi" dataset is characterized by its diverse content, comprising books from the 16th to the 20th centuries, written in Latin, French, and other languages. The pages within each book exhibit a high level of variability, with uneven backgrounds, uneven writing, and varying font sizes. Moreover, the text includes numerous forms of handwriting, with words often connected and words missing, presenting a highly complex challenge for both handwritten text correction and traditional machine recognition tasks. The proposed approach and associated resources can facilitate the development and evaluation of advanced machine learning techniques for handwritten text recognition, particularly in the domain of historical document analysis. Despite several optimizations, efficient memory allocation on GPUs with minimal overhead remains a challenge. To address this issue, we introduce DynaSOAr, a highly efficient and adaptable memory allocator for object-oriented programming in parallel environments. Built upon dynamic memory allocation, DynaSOAr incorporates a frame pool and a cache to minimize memory usage and reduce fragmentation, thus optimizing memory access for various data structures and operations. Our experiments demonstrate that DynaSOAr outperforms current allocators by up to 60% and achieves a 2x speed improvement, especially when combined with other optimizations. Additionally, we provide a framework for a comprehensive evaluation of memory allocators, allowing for a detailed analysis of their performance and characteristics. This evaluation identifies key factors that influence memory allocation and guides the development of more efficient allocators. To further enable research in this area, we make our allocator and evaluation framework open-source, allowing the community to contribute and compare different allocators. Our experiments reveal that a simple and general-purpose allocator can be more efficient than specialized allocators, thus highlighting the importance of a comprehensive evaluation and a shared benchmark suite. Our work enables researchers to study memory allocation and empowers developers to create more efficient parallel applications using our allocator and evaluation framework. Our hybrid allocator successfully runs on both CPUs and GPUs, demonstrating a general applicability and versatility. In various fields, ensuring decision-making policies are resilient to uncertain conditions is of utmost importance. Probabilistic risk assessment and management techniques have been developed, with Bayesian networks as a popular tool for analyzing and mitigating risks. From a Bayesian perspective, the uncertainty surrounding system variables can be quantified by credal Bayesian networks, which utilize confidence intervals to measure epistemic uncertainty. We've identified and analyzed a family of metrics known as the Tversky metrics, where the base space is the power set of any given finite set $X$. The metrics in this family are determined by three parameters: a weight for the presence of shared elements $w_{\mathrm{prec}}$, a weight for the presence of unique elements $w_{\mathrm{rec}}$, and a weight that adjusts the scaling of the metric $w_{\phi}$. When $w_{\mathrm{prec}}$, $w_{\mathrm{rec}}$, and $w_{\phi}$ are set to $\frac{1}{2}$, $\frac{1}{2}$, and $1$, respectively, the metric is equivalent to the Jaccard distance between the elements of $X$. By adjusting these parameters, the metric also takes on characteristics similar to those of the inverse difference distance, a normalized version of the information distance between elements of $X$. The family's properties, including those related to the stability and continuity of the metric, as well as the uniqueness of its solution to which the metric converges, have been proven and verified. Additionally, the minimum and maximum possible values of the metric have been quantified in terms of the parameters $w_{\mathrm{prec}}$ and $w_{\mathrm{rec}}$. Our analysis has further shown that the metric induces a topologically consistent distance function on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $X$. A software implementation of the metric, which has been named the Tversky metric, is also provided. It has been written in Python and is documented in the provided code. The Python code in the listed reference has been used to generate the figures included in the presented research. Due to the versatility of the parameters governing the Tversky metric, this metric can be easily adapted and applied across a wide range of domains and use cases, including but not limited to information retrieval, where it was first encountered, bioinformatics, and machine learning. A comprehensive evaluation of the efficacy of the Tversky metric in these domains and others has been carried out and is documented in the provided research. Specifically, it has been observed that the Tversky metric can be an effective choice for tasks in which both precision and recall are significant considerations. On the other hand, when recovery is deemed more important than precision, the Jaccard metric may be a more suitable option. Hadwiger's Coloring Conjecture asserts that every graph with t colors can be divided into a union of t complete subgraphs. Our research presents two sets of evidence supporting this idea. First, we demonstrate that the majority of graphs with 4 and 5 colors comply with Hadwiger's notion. Specifically, in the case of 4 colors, our result is an extension of Mynhardt and Mynhardt's work (published in 2015), while for 5 colors, it builds upon Mubungira's findings (published in 2018). Our approach employs a combination of mathematical analysis and the application of lemmas to partition graphs into specific subgraphs. Second, we developed an efficient algorithm to determine whether a given graph meets the criteria of Hadwiger's conjecture, particularly in graphs with 4 colors, and this algorithm could also be used for 5 colors. This problem was previously addressed by Mubungira in a program he developed (also containing tests), which, although capable of solving some instances, had limitations in others and had a high time complexity of O(n^5), where n represents the number of vertices in the graph. In contrast, our algorithm has a significantly lower time complexity of O(n^2) for both 4 and 5 colors. Our research also includes the creation of a computer system that can quickly determine the graph divisions required for Hadwiger's conjecture in the majority of graphs. This system can handle a wide range of graph sizes and has tested over 1.4 billion graphs with 4 colors and over 1.3 billion graphs with 5 colors. This technology is now available online. Finally, in an effort to make our research more accessible, we have included detailed step-by-step explanations of our methods as well as the underlying mathematical theories used in the proof. These explanations, along with the associated code, can be found on our website. The associated code can be found at https://bitbucket.org/charlesmubungira/hadwiger-graph-divisions. Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) have seen widespread adoption across various domains, but their inner workings remain largely opaque. In contrast, Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs) are particularly difficult to interpret due to their application in graph-structured data. To better understand GCNNs, researchers typically employ visualization methods such as analyzing the graph convolution operation. Despite numerous visualizations and feature attribution techniques, the underlying rationale behind GCNNs remains unclear. This study presents an alternative approach where the graph convolution operation is approximated by matching the structure of GCNN-based classifiers with that of traditional DNNs. By doing so, we develop a simplified and intuitive understanding of the graph convolution operation, revealing its equivalence to a multi-layer perceptron. This method offers several benefits, including the ability to bypass the need for visualizing the graph convolution operation and enabling the use of established DNN interpretability techniques. As a result, we can now directly analyze the effect of each node feature on the model's decision, similar to how this is done in standard DNNs. Furthermore, our method allows for the exploration of GCNNs without requiring an explicit graph topology, thereby expanding the scope of applications for GCNNs. To validate our approach, we conduct experiments across multiple benchmark datasets, where the results show that our method surpasses the performance of existing GCNN and visual interpretation techniques. A recently developed neural dependency parsing method has achieved remarkable results across various languages and domains. However, its high reliance on large, annotated datasets has proven costly and impractical to obtain. To address this issue, our proposed self-training approach leverages the parser's own outputs to create pseudo-labels for unseen data points, effectively expanding the training dataset with semantically accurate annotations. To optimize the annotation process, we've integrated a enhanced dependency parsing model that combines the original model and a syntax-aware language model, allowing for a greater volume of pseudo-labels to be generated while minimizing errors. Furthermore, we've developed a novel strategy for pseudo-tree selection, which prioritizes trees that maximize parsing accuracy and facilitate generalization. Our results have shown that this self-training technique, when applied across multiple iterations, can substantially improve parsing accuracy on low-resource languages, ultimately reaching levels comparable to those of parser-dependent approaches. Specifically, our research has demonstrated parsing accuracy increases of 1.47% and 0.95% on the English and Chinese datasets, respectively, following each self-training iteration. To validate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, we've conducted experiments on English and Chinese datasets of varying sizes, from 50K to 15M annotations. Our results have consistently shown that self-training yields significant gains across all low-resource and medium-resource language scenarios. Furthermore, our research has provided a deeper understanding of the behavior of neural dependency parsers on low-resource languages, revealing that self-training can mitigate the adverse effects of limited training data on parsing performance. To facilitate the reproduction of our results, we've released our implemented code, as well as the necessary data processing tools, on public repositories. Our research has further established the feasibility of applying self-training to neural dependency parsing, thereby enabling the parsing of low-resource languages with high accuracy. To achieve this, we've successfully adapted and combined concepts from natural language inference and dependency parsing. Our results have shown that self-training can be effectively applied across languages with rich contextualized representations, as well as those lacking such features. Our analysis reveals increasing electron localization around the 10% Bi content threshold, as indicated by the shift of the Ir L3 edge towards higher binding energies and the emergence of a near-surface charge gap. Our findings are consistent with the hypothesis that this phase of the pyrochlore iridates undergoes an insulator-to-metal phase transition, where the critical Bi concentration is heavily influenced by doping-induced disorder. Moreover, our surface analysis leveraged a synchrotron light source and revealed a near-surface charge gap, in addition to an in-depth examination of the chemical composition and the impact of surface effects. Ultimately, our study highlights the benefits of combining SXPS with other synchrotron-based techniques to gain a deeper understanding of the complex behavior of correlated materials. By employing a highly surface-sensitive approach, our study sheds light on the electronic properties within the (Eu_1-xBi_x)_2Ir2O7 series and offers a detailed examination of the electronic behavior near the surface, an aspect that is often overlooked in bulk analysis. As such, our work is expected to have far-reaching implications for the understanding and development of pyrochlore iridates as potential hosts of quantum phases and spin liquids. These configurations often incur a performance cost, so a higher number of users usually requires a greater allocation of resources. In shared environments, this can lead to a conflict over resources, making it difficult for some users to use the program at all. To address this issue, our study investigates a novel approach where the program's memory configuration is optimized based on the user's needs during compilation, rather than at run-time. By doing so, we minimize the program's memory usage and ensure that users with different requirements can coexist without competing for resources. Through an in-depth analysis, we identified several benefits associated with this approach, highlighted the challenges of applying it to dynamic settings, and proposed potential solutions for future research. Measuring inter-beat intervals (IBI) from ECG signals is a crucial task in assessing heart function and detecting cardiac disorders. The analysis of IBI can indicate irregular heart rhythms, heart rate changes, and other conditions. Previous studies have employed deep learning models, such as long short-term memory (LSTM) and recurrent neural networks (RNN), to estimate IBI from ECG signals. Despite their success, these models are characterized by complex architecture, a large number of trainable parameters, and slow convergence, making them difficult to implement and optimize. In an effort to improve IBI estimation and overcome these limitations, a novel approach using the Tiramisu model is proposed. The Tiramisu model leverages a custom architecture with a reduced number of trainable parameters, thereby facilitating efficient training and optimization. By incorporating residual learning and non-local block techniques, the model can focus on estimating IBI values and eliminate noise from the ECG signal. The model's efficacy was evaluated in terms of mean absolute error (MAE) and was compared with LSTM and RNN models under various testing conditions. The results indicate that the Tiramisu model outperforms LSTM and RNN models in all testing scenarios, demonstrating its versatility and potential applications. Furthermore, the study examines the effect of signal length on IBI estimation and investigates the models' generalization capability when the signal length differs from that used in training. The proposed approach shows promise in the field of heart rate estimation and can be adapted to various signal processing applications. Additionally, the study's findings can guide researchers in selecting suitable models for signal-dependent applications and understanding the models' behavior when the signal properties differ from those used in training. The code and data used in this study are available for review and replication, providing a valuable resource for the community. The models' source code can be accessed at the following link: https://github.com/ahmed-omar/heart-rate-estimation. The data used in this study can be obtained from the following link: https://endophysio.org/physio.html. The primary goal of HUMBI is to enhance the performance of 3D human modeling and reconstruction. The dataset showcases a diverse set of human poses via 8 viewpoints, along with accurately fitted clothing patterns that serve as visual representations of body expressions. To validate the HUMBI dataset and evaluate reconstruction methods, a benchmark challenge has been established. Despite the growing need for non-English models, NLP models often can't be directly applied to other languages due to limited data or performance issues. We present a new approach that allows information from a task-trained in one language to benefit a task of the same type in another language, without needing parallel data or extensive manual labeling. We use neural task representations to bridge the language gap and achieve this model-agnostic transfer through a general task representation method, allowing for easy adaptation to new languages and tasks. Our transfer framework can be applied to both NMT and machine translation, and we test it on two cross-lingual transfer scenarios: zero-shot and non-zero-shot transfers. Our experiments show that our framework can successfully transfer knowledge across languages and achieve significant improvements, up to 9.5 MVC, depending on the language pair and task. Our code is available online. 

The key contributions of this work are:
  1. A model-agnostic approach to neural cross-lingual transfer.
  2. Using neural task representations to facilitate this transfer.
  3: A language-independent task representation method that can be applied to any NLP task.
  4: Applying this representation to knowledge transfer across different sentence forms while maintaining the same semantic meaning.
  5: Testing our framework on multiple language pairs and evaluating its performance using three NLP tasks, achieving notable results. 
  6: Showcasing the transfer framework's ability to be applied to both NMT and machine translation, as well as its robustness across various settings. 
  7: Outlining potential future research directions and areas of improvement for NLP models. 
  8: Making our code available for reproducibility. 

In the future, we can enhance our transfer framework in several ways, such as incorporating more task representations, exploring other forms of knowledge transfer, and developing more sophisticated sentence forms. Additionally, we can investigate the role of word order in NLP tasks and push the boundaries of NLP model development.

To bridge the quality gap between low-resolution video and high-definition content, researchers developed video super-resolution techniques, increasing compressed video quality through analysis and reorganization. A recent approach, BasicVSR, achieved superior performance with minimal computational requirements by using a conditional propagation network, temporal fusion module, and self-aligning mechanism. However, the original method suffered from underutilizing spatial information and inaccurate feature alignment within frames. This study addresses these issues in BasicVSR through the introduction of multi-path network architecture, a feature correlation alignment mechanism, and a resource-allocatable fusion module. The proposed model, BasicVSR++, enhances the basic framework with additional spatial features, a feature correlation mechanism, and a flexible fusion module. Experimental results demonstrate the improved quality and compact model of BasicVSR++, achieving top rankings in various video enhancement competitions and surpassing several prominent VRNet and CSF-based models in several benchmark datasets. Notably, the method shows significant reduction in parameters and operations while maintaining a higher quality output. The authors provide an in-depth analysis of the results, model interpretations, and provide a benchmark for future research. The source code is available on the GitHub platform (https://github.com/heyuhuanyu/BasicVSR++).

In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly benefit from knowledge gained in one task to benefit another. However, when using a single policy network for all tasks, learning one task can sometimes interfere with learning the others. Our research focuses on how this interference affects model-based multi-task reinforcement learning and finds that it is prevented in this setting. By allowing a task-specific policy to be learned for each experience, the model can easily select the desired task without being affected by others. Our findings also reveal that using a modular structure has other benefits, including reducing the required amount of experience and improving performance when tasks have different reward structures. Overall, our results show that using a modular approach can greatly improve learning in model-based multi-task reinforcement learning. Additionally, our method is applicable not just to reinforcement learning, but also to solving optimal control problems when goals are unknown, providing a universal feature for handling diverse goal-conditional problems. A demonstration of our method is available online. This research was a key part of an academic thesis and has been presented at the 2020 IJCAI conference. It has been published in the 2021 proceedings of the same conference, under the title "Modular Networks Prevent Catastrophic Interference in Model-Based Multi-Task Reinforcement Learning". Our proof utilizes a novel approach based on subharmonic function properties and the Poisson integral formula. Additionally, we discuss the connections between the obtained results and potential-theoretic issues in the mentioned example. The provided example also highlights the utility of combining classical potential theory and Clifford algebra techniques to address analysis issues in the context of R^n+1 space. We identify two specific cases where these maps exhibit maximal entropy invariant measures, which can be represented by binary and ternary codes. Additionally, we provide numerical evidence suggesting that the entropy of these measures approaches the maximum possible for the 2D and 3D spaces as the parameter values change. Furthermore, we outline a mechanism to explain why this occurs, which may aid in broadening the scope of the entropy approach for simplifying complex dynamical systems. We also observe that the entropy of these measures is directly linked to the amount of chaos present in the systems, as indicated by the average rate of change of entropy as a function of the parameter. We derive analytical formulas for the entropy of the measures in the 2D case and present numerical results for the 3D case. Moreover, we establish a connection between the maximal entropy measures of the 2D generalized baker map and the Dyck system, which is a well-studied 1D map, and provide numerical evidence for the related entropy approachability problem in the 1D, 2D, and 3D settings. This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet to produce raw audio data. Leveraging the benefits of autoregressive models and pitch-dependent dilated convolutional neural networks, the quasi-periodic model mimics the natural patterns found in speech and music. Experimental outcomes with the LJ Speech dataset reveal that the quasi-periodic model achieves comparable mean opinion scores to the standard WaveNet model, while demonstrating improved distribution accuracy and naturalness metrics. Notably, the quasi-periodic model exhibits enhanced robustness against pitch shift transformations. To facilitate real-time inference, a compact version of the quasi-periodic model was created using convolutional autoencoders and weight averaging techniques. The resulting model shows a 6 times speed increase. Our source code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/uis-speech/quasi-periodic-wavenet. Evaluations with the CMU AR Voice dataset reveal that the quasi-periodic model produces more coherent speech even after being subjected to intense background noise. A comparison of the quasi-periodic model with the Tacotron text-to-speech system was also conducted, yielding a mean opinion score of 3.75 for the quasi-periodic model, thereby setting a new benchmark for speech synthesis. Building upon the quasi-periodic model, we have initiated a new research thread that combines this model with sequence-to-sequence frameworks to achieve state-of-the-art results in speech synthesis. Key aspects of this new approach include using pitch-dependent dilated convolutional neural networks in the generative model and employing a pitch extraction algorithm based on the strong correlation between pitch and spectral flatness measure. This novel method has achieved mean opinion scores of 4.23 and 4.35 for fine-grained and coarse-grained pitch extraction respectively. Moreover, we have achieved a mean opinion score of 4.57 for speech synthesized without pitch errors. A detailed description of this research is included in a companion paper. Recommender Systems built with Collaborative Filtering (CF) have become indispensable for their ability to address the overwhelming information issue and the impossibly vast item space. However, their effectiveness is hampered when dealing with new users and items with no rating history. To enhance CF's capabilities, this research proposes an innovative CF approach called BiCLF, centered on the concept of user-specific biclusters to produce more accurate recommendations. BiCLF recognizes that users' preferences exhibit two interconnected aspects: the specific group each user belongs to and the items within that group. By identifying and honoring these biclusters, BiCLF acknowledges the localized, sparse, and subjective nature of user preferences. Through practical transformations, BiCLF transforms these aspects into two CF-compatible sub-problems, allowing for the discovery of biclusters and the prediction of user preferences. By integrating these two components, BiCLF outperforms state-of-the-art CF methods in two real-world recommender systems. Furthermore, BiCLF offers actionable insights into user preferences and their underlying group structures. To facilitate replication, the code and data used in this research are made available for download. BiCLF's focus on biclusters also enables the exploration of preference subjectivity, adding a fresh perspective to the CF field. By analyzing user preferences within their group contexts, BiCLF uncovers insights into user preference patterns and their underlying structures. To replicate these results, the code and data used in this research are made available for download. This technical report showcases the winning model of the AQTC task, recently introduced in the LOVEU challenge at CVPR 2022, where the goal is to generate multi-step responses by processing multiple input prompts in sequence. The LoveU dataset comprises a collection of multi-round conversations between two individuals. The researchers behind this study identified that standard language models are not capable of effectively processing sequential input prompts due to the limitations of self-attention mechanisms, which prevent the encoding of long sequences. To overcome this challenge, the researchers proposed a solution involving the division of the sequence into shorter segments and the use of a stack-based architecture to process these segments in a sequential manner. The winning model was further enhanced through the incorporation of additional modules, including a module that utilizes the context to guide the selection of relevant segments, and two modules that facilitate the retrieval and incorporation of relevant context information. The model was evaluated on the LoveU dataset, which comprises 98M tokens, and processed through a data pipeline involving four stages, including pre-training, tuning, in-stage tuning, and re-tuning. The model was fine-tuned in an AQTC manner, with the goal of generating multi-step responses. The report outlines the technical details of the winning model and highlights its performance through numerical evaluations, including a comparison with eight other prominent baselines. The results indicate that the proposed model outperformed these baselines by a significant margin, achieving a 0.4% improvement in response accuracy and a 13.6% improvement in response length. The winning model was made available through an open-source repository, and the associated code can be accessed via this URL: https://github.com/whaiwhai/CVPR-LOVEU-AQTC. A fundamental theory known as active inference underpins how living beings interact with their surroundings. This theory views the brain as an efficient tool that employs prior knowledge and available sensory information to create a detailed, realistic framework of the world. Furthermore, it is believed that this framework is not merely a static concept but rather a dynamic entity that is constantly updated as new data becomes available. Prior studies utilized simplified computational methods to investigate the application of active inference in simulated environments; however, these approaches face challenges such as the limitations of their computational intensity, the simplicity of their models, and the difficulty of adapting to novel situations. To address these concerns, we propose a deep active inference approach that incorporates a detailed 3D representation of the environment and utilizes deep neural networks, thereby enabling more sophisticated modeling of the world. This method is put to use in a real-world autonomous robot navigation system, where it successfully acquires a detailed understanding of its surroundings and navigates through unfamiliar areas while avoiding obstacles. Our approach represents a significant advancement in the application of active inference, as it demonstrates the capability of using this framework to create advanced, learned models of the world that can be employed in practical robotic systems. Additionally, our study highlights the potential of active inference to generate representations that are rich in semantic meaning, thereby paving the way for more advanced applications in robotics and other fields. Event identification is crucial in various real-world applications such as disaster monitoring, traffic surveillance, and research into social movements. Most current approaches for detecting events rely on static graph representations of nodes and edges between nodes over time. However, this methodology has two significant limitations. First, it fails to capture relationships between distant nodes that may arise at different times. Second, it often results in overly broad event detection as most node patterns are considered. To address these shortcomings, we propose a new framework that uses a holographic graph representation to represent interactions between nodes over time. Our approach, called Temporal Link Prediction for Event Detection (TLPE), not only considers relationships between nearby nodes but also those that may be farther apart, connected by intermediate nodes. We evaluate TLPE on three real-world datasets and compare it to alternative methods, demonstrating its superior performance and more accurate event detection. Our results show that TLPE not only identifies more events but also reduces false positives compared to other approaches. The growing presence of artificial intelligence systems has led to a significant rise in the need for their explanations. Transparency and stakeholder trust are achieved by reducing the opacity of these systems through the provision of explanations. In this paper, we will explore the interconnection between explainable AI and requirements engineering. The challenges in the XAI field will be highlighted and solutions proposed, with a framework and future research directions on how requirements engineering can aid in addressing these difficulties. A particular approach is presented that views explainability as a user-centric requirement, allowing for more effective stakeholder needs to be identified and met. By recognizing that explanations have various purposes, audiences, and creation methods, AI systems' explainability can be enhanced. Consequently, a simpler, more approachable process can be implemented for specifying and achieving this explainability. This approach may offer a more accessible entry point for researchers and practitioners to understand and address the explainability gap. It also has the potential to foster a more comprehensive understanding of AI transparency by promoting a multifaceted requirement for XAI. By reflecting on these complexities, progress can be made in the required transparency of AI, ultimately leading to more reliable and trustworthy AI for all stakeholders. This document provides a summary of the content from a course held at Stanford University in the spring of 2018.  The course brings together insights from cognitive neuroscience and systems neuroscience to create intelligent systems by combining human and machine intelligence.  The course uses a tangible example - a digital assistant that learns and evolves through ongoing conversations with an experienced software engineer while beginning as an effective analytical and problem-solving tool.  Over time, these intelligent assistants develop essential thinking strategies and learn to rely on intuition, eventually becoming invaluable creative assets in their field.  Amanuensis, an implementation of this concept based on dialogues between a human and a computer, is provided as an open-source resource for exploring this idea.  By using a dialogue interface, the program and its human partner collaborate to translate high-level ideas into specific programming tasks and analyze error logs to pinpoint areas where the assistant can improve its understanding by learning from its mistakes.  By iteratively refining its capabilities through self-improvement, the program becomes an indispensable partner for the human, serving as a smart tool that's aware of its own strengths and weaknesses.  By integrating insights from both neuroscience and computer science, the program and its human partner can work together as a cohesive team, leveraging each other's skills to achieve better results through mutual collaboration.  Amanuensis is now available for public use on the GitHub platform at the following address: https://github.com/amanuensis-stanford/amanuensis.  By utilizing this open-source resource, developers can create their own intelligent assistants that learn and grow alongside them as they work, leading to innovative breakthroughs in a variety of fields.
